units.3: Fungi, viruses, disinfectants and sterility testing

short.q: Define microbiology. Write its branches and scope in pharmacy.
short.hi: Microbiology = सूक्ष्म जीवों (bacteria, fungi, virus) का अध्ययन

kp.t: Study of microorganisms too small for naked eye

short.a:
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses, protozoa, algae) that are too small to be seen with the naked eye.
Branches: bacteriology, virology, mycology, protozoology, immunology; applied branches like medical, industrial, food, environmental and pharmaceutical microbiology.
Scope in pharmacy: production of antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes and vitamins by fermentation; sterilization and sterility testing of products; microbiological assay of antibiotics and vitamins; control of contamination and spoilage; preservative evaluation; biotechnology and cell culture.

short.q: Write a short note on the history of microbiology (contributions of Leeuwenhoek, Pasteur and Koch).
short.hi: Leeuwenhoek ने microscope से पहली बार bacteria देखे
short.a:
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (17th century) made simple microscopes and first described microorganisms, calling them 'animalcules'; he is called the father of microbiology/bacteriology.
Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation using swan-neck flasks, introduced pasteurization, studied fermentation and developed vaccines (anthrax, rabies).
Robert Koch proved the germ theory of disease, gave Koch's postulates, isolated anthrax, tubercle and cholera bacilli and introduced solid media.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid (phenol).

short.q: Give the morphological classification of bacteria with examples.
short.hi: आकार के आधार पर: cocci (गोल), bacilli (छड़), spiral

kp.t: Arrangements: diplo, strepto, staphylo, tetrad, sarcina

short.a:
Bacteria are classified by shape:
1. Cocci (spherical): diplococci (pairs, Pneumococcus), streptococci (chains), staphylococci (grape-like clusters), tetrads and sarcinae (cubes of 8).
2. Bacilli (rod shaped): e.g. Escherichia coli, Bacillus subtilis; coccobacilli are short rods.
3. Vibrios (comma shaped): Vibrio cholerae.
4. Spirilla (rigid spiral): Spirillum.
5. Spirochaetes (flexible spiral): Treponema, Leptospira.
6. Others: actinomycetes (branched filaments), mycoplasma (no cell wall, pleomorphic).

short.q: Write a short note on the bacterial cell wall of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
short.hi: Gram +ve में मोटी peptidoglycan परत, Gram -ve में पतली + outer membrane

kp.t: Functions: shape, rigidity, protects from osmotic lysis

short.a:
The cell wall gives shape and rigidity and protects the cell from osmotic lysis. Its main component is peptidoglycan (murein): chains of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by peptides.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan layer (many layers) with teichoic and lipoteichoic acids; little lipid.
Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan layer in the periplasmic space, covered by an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin), lipoproteins and porins; high lipid content.
Penicillins and lysozyme act on peptidoglycan.

short.q: What are the nutritional requirements of bacteria? Classify bacteria based on nutrition.
short.hi: Bacteria को carbon, nitrogen, energy source और growth factors चाहिए
short.a:
Bacteria need water, a carbon source, a nitrogen source, an energy source, minerals (P, S, K, Mg, Fe, Ca, trace elements) and sometimes growth factors (vitamins, amino acids, purines, pyrimidines).
Classification:
- By carbon source: autotrophs (use CO2) and heterotrophs (use organic compounds; most pathogens).
- By energy source: phototrophs (light) and chemotrophs (chemical oxidation).
- By electron donor: lithotrophs (inorganic) and organotrophs (organic).
Combined: photoautotrophs, chemoautotrophs, chemoheterotrophs (most medically important bacteria).

short.q: What are culture media? Classify culture media with examples.
short.hi: Culture media = bacteria उगाने का nutrient मिश्रण

kp.t: Nutrient preparation to grow microbes in lab

short.a:
Culture media are nutrient preparations used to grow microorganisms in the laboratory.
By consistency: liquid (broth), semisolid (about 0.5% agar) and solid (about 1.5-2% agar).
By composition: synthetic/defined media (known chemicals) and complex/non-synthetic media (peptone, meat extract).
By purpose: basal (nutrient broth/agar), enriched (blood agar, chocolate agar), enrichment (selenite F broth), selective (MacConkey agar, Wilson-Blair, Lowenstein-Jensen), differential/indicator (MacConkey distinguishes lactose fermenters), transport media (Stuart's), anaerobic media (Robertson's cooked meat, thioglycollate) and assay media.

short.q: Write the raw materials used in culture media and their functions.
short.hi: Peptone (nitrogen), agar (जमाने वाला), meat extract, yeast extract

kp.t: Meat extract / yeast extract: vitamins, minerals

short.a:
Peptone: partially digested protein; supplies amino acids and nitrogen.
Meat (beef) extract: supplies amino acids, vitamins, mineral salts and carbohydrate.
Yeast extract: rich source of B-vitamins and growth factors.
Agar: complex polysaccharide from red seaweeds; solidifying agent, melts about 95°C and sets about 42°C; not used as nutrient by most bacteria.
Sodium chloride and other salts: maintain osmotic balance, supply electrolytes.
Carbohydrates (glucose, lactose): energy source and fermentation tests.
Blood, serum, egg: enrichment for fastidious organisms.
Water: distilled or deionized. Indicators and buffers: show pH change.

short.q: Write the physical parameters affecting bacterial growth.
short.hi: Temperature, pH, oxygen, osmotic pressure, light growth को प्रभावित करते हैं
short.a:
Temperature: psychrophiles (optimum below 20°C), mesophiles (20-45°C, optimum 37°C for most pathogens), thermophiles (above 45°C).
Oxygen: obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes, microaerophiles and aerotolerant organisms.
pH: most pathogens grow best at pH 7.2-7.6; acidophiles and alkaliphiles prefer extremes.
Osmotic pressure: most need isotonic conditions; halophiles need high salt.
Moisture: water is essential; drying stops growth.
Carbon dioxide: capnophiles need extra CO2 (5-10%).
Light: UV light is harmful; phototrophs need light.

short.q: What is a pure culture? Write the methods of isolation of pure culture.
short.hi: Pure culture = एक ही प्रकार के bacteria की culture
short.a:
A pure culture contains only one species (strain) of microorganism, usually derived from a single cell/colony.
Methods of isolation:
1. Streak plate: inoculum is streaked with a loop over an agar plate in sections so that isolated colonies form.
2. Pour plate: serial dilutions are mixed with molten cooled agar and poured; colonies grow within and on agar.
3. Spread plate: a small diluted volume is spread on the agar surface with a sterile L-shaped spreader.
4. Serial dilution method.
5. Enrichment and selective media, single-cell (micromanipulator) technique.

short.q: Write the methods of preservation of pure cultures.
short.hi: Culture को लंबे समय तक बचाने के लिए lyophilization, refrigeration

kp.t: Deep freezing / liquid nitrogen (-196°C) with glycerol

short.a:
Pure cultures are preserved to keep them viable and genetically stable:
1. Periodic subculturing onto fresh media.
2. Refrigeration at 4°C (short term, weeks).
3. Overlaying slants with sterile mineral (paraffin) oil, reducing drying and metabolism (months to years).
4. Freezing at -20°C or -70°C with glycerol as cryoprotectant.
5. Lyophilization (freeze drying): culture is frozen and water removed under vacuum; sealed ampoules last many years; best method.
6. Storage in liquid nitrogen at -196°C.
7. Drying in sterile soil or sand (spore-formers and fungi).

short.q: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
short.hi: Prokaryote में true nucleus नहीं होता, eukaryote में होता है

kp.t: Prokaryote: no true nucleus / no nuclear membrane

short.a:
Prokaryotes (bacteria): no true nucleus; DNA lies free as a nucleoid without nuclear membrane; single circular chromosome; 70S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, ER, Golgi); cell wall contains peptidoglycan; divide by binary fission; size about 1-10 µm.
Eukaryotes (fungi, protozoa, algae, animal and plant cells): true nucleus with nuclear membrane; many linear chromosomes with histones; 80S ribosomes (70S in mitochondria); membrane-bound organelles present; cell wall, if present, of cellulose or chitin; divide by mitosis/meiosis; larger, about 10-100 µm.

short.q: Draw and explain the bacterial growth curve.
short.hi: Growth curve के चार phase: lag, log, stationary, decline

kp.t: Log/exponential phase: rapid division, constant generation time
Stationary phase: growth = death, nutrients exhausted
Plot of log number of cells vs time

short.a:
When bacteria are inoculated into a fresh liquid medium and the log of viable count is plotted against time, a growth curve with four phases is obtained:
1. Lag phase: cells adapt, synthesize enzymes, increase in size; little or no division.
2. Log (exponential) phase: cells divide at constant maximum rate; generation time is shortest; cells most sensitive to antibiotics.
3. Stationary phase: nutrients exhausted and toxic products accumulate; rate of division equals rate of death; spores and secondary metabolites (antibiotics) form.
4. Decline (death) phase: death exceeds division; viable count falls.

short.q: Write the methods of cultivation of anaerobic bacteria.
short.hi: Anaerobes को oxygen रहित माहौल चाहिए: McIntosh-Fildes jar

kp.t: Reducing media: thioglycollate, Robertson's cooked meat

short.a:
Anaerobes are killed or inhibited by oxygen, so oxygen must be excluded.
Methods:
1. Reducing media: sodium thioglycollate broth, Robertson's cooked meat medium (glutathione, cysteine), with resazurin as redox indicator.
2. McIntosh and Fildes anaerobic jar: air is replaced with hydrogen; a palladium catalyst combines H2 with residual O2 to form water; methylene blue indicator stays colourless when anaerobic.
3. Gas-Pak system: sachet releases H2 and CO2 when water is added.
4. Anaerobic chambers/glove box, deep agar shake culture, Buchner's method (alkaline pyrogallol absorbs O2).

short.q: Differentiate between total count and viable count of bacteria.
short.hi: Total count में जीवित+मृत, viable count में केवल जीवित cells गिने जाते हैं

kp.t: Total count counts live + dead cells
Total: turbidity, Coulter counter, dry weight
Viable count: only living cells forming colonies
Viable: plate count, CFU per mL

short.a:
Total count measures all cells, living and dead.
Methods: direct microscopic count using a Petroff-Hausser counting chamber or haemocytometer, electronic Coulter counter, turbidity (spectrophotometer/nephelometer), dry weight and nitrogen content.
Viable count measures only living cells able to multiply.
Methods: pour plate or spread plate count after serial dilution (colonies counted, result as colony forming units, CFU/mL; plates with 30-300 colonies chosen), membrane filtration count, and most probable number (MPN) method.
Total count is quick; viable count is slower (incubation) but tells the number of live organisms.

short.q: Describe isolation of pure cultures from contaminated pharmaceutical samples.
short.hi: Contaminated sample → dilution → selective media → single colony → subculture → identify

kp.t: Aseptic sampling and neutralisation of preservative
Streak / pour / spread plate to get isolated colonies
Selective and differential media (MacConkey, SDA, mannitol salt)
Pick single colony and subculture to purity
Confirm purity by Gram stain and identify (biochemical tests)

a.intro: Pharmaceutical samples (raw materials, water, syrups, creams, tablets) may carry mixed contaminants. To identify them, each organism must first be obtained as a pure culture, i.e. a population arising from a single cell.
points: Sampling and preparation: sample taken aseptically; dissolved or suspended in a diluent (buffered sodium chloride-peptone, pH 7.0); preservative activity neutralised with lecithin and polysorbate 80 (or by dilution/membrane filtration); creams dispersed with sterile surfactant.
Enrichment (if needed): incubate in enrichment broths for specified organisms, e.g. soybean casein digest broth, then MacConkey broth for E. coli, Rappaport for Salmonella.
Serial dilution (1:10, 1:100, 1:1000) so that individual cells are separated.

Plating: streak plate (quadrant streaking), pour plate or spread plate on general (soybean casein digest agar) and selective/differential media: MacConkey (E. coli), mannitol salt (S. aureus), cetrimide (Pseudomonas aeruginosa), XLD (Salmonella), Sabouraud dextrose agar (fungi).
Isolation: after incubation (30-35°C bacteria, 20-25°C fungi), a well-separated colony of each type is picked and restreaked on fresh medium until colonies are uniform.
Purity check and identification: uniform colony morphology, Gram stain, then biochemical tests (catalase, coagulase, oxidase, IMViC) or automated systems; preserve the isolate.
a.diagram: Draw a Petri plate with quadrant streaking (4 zones) showing heavy growth in zone 1 and isolated colonies in zone 4, with an arrow to a fresh slant labelled 'subculture'.
a.conclusion: Pure isolates allow correct identification of contaminants, tracing their source and corrective action in manufacturing.

short.q: State one diagnostic limitation of acid-fast staining.
short.hi: Acid-fast stain सभी acid-fast organisms को एक जैसा लाल दिखाता है

kp.t: Not specific: other acid-fast organisms also stain red
Cannot tell live from dead bacilli
Low sensitivity: needs about 10,000 bacilli per mL

short.a: Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining only shows that red bacilli with mycolic acid are present. It is not specific: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, M. leprae, non-tuberculous mycobacteria and partly Nocardia all appear red, so the species cannot be identified (culture or molecular tests are needed). It also cannot tell live from dead bacilli, and its sensitivity is low, since about 10,000 bacilli per mL of sputum are needed for a positive smear.

short.q: Why is IMViC testing important in pharmaceutical water systems?
short.hi: IMViC से E. coli (faecal contamination) और Enterobacter में फर्क होता है

kp.t: E. coli is a specified/objectionable organism that must be absent

short.a: Pharmaceutical water can be contaminated by coliform bacteria. IMViC (Indole, Methyl red, Voges-Proskauer, Citrate) differentiates Escherichia coli (++--) from Enterobacter/Klebsiella (--++). E. coli is an indicator of faecal (sewage) contamination and is a specified objectionable organism that must be absent from purified water and oral products as per pharmacopoeias. So IMViC helps trace the source of contamination and decide corrective action on the water system.

short.q: Define SAL (sterility assurance level) with reference to regulatory compliance.
short.hi: SAL = sterilization के बाद एक भी जीवित microbe बचने की probability

kp.t: Probability of one viable microorganism surviving on a unit
Shown by validation, not by sterility test alone

short.a: Sterility assurance level (SAL) is the probability of a single viable microorganism being present on an item after sterilization. Regulatory bodies (pharmacopoeias, FDA, EU GMP) require an SAL of 10^-6 or better for terminally sterilized products, i.e. not more than one non-sterile unit in a million. SAL is proved by validation of the sterilization cycle (D-value, bioburden, biological indicators), because the sterility test on a few samples cannot detect such low levels.

short.q: Mention one safety concern associated with ethylene oxide sterilization.
short.hi: EtO ज़हरीली, carcinogenic और explosive गैस है

kp.t: Toxic residues: ethylene chlorohydrin, ethylene glycol
Mixed with CO2 to reduce fire risk

short.a: Ethylene oxide is toxic, irritant, mutagenic and carcinogenic to workers, and it is highly flammable and explosive when mixed with air (about 3-80%). It also leaves toxic residues (EtO, ethylene chlorohydrin, ethylene glycol) in plastics and rubber, so products need a long aeration (degassing) period before use. To reduce fire risk it is used diluted with carbon dioxide or other inert gases in closed chambers.

short.q: Why is heat fixing and heating during staining needed in the Ziehl-Neelsen method?
short.hi: Mycolic acid (waxy wall) के कारण stain अंदर जाने के लिए heat चाहिए

kp.t: Mycobacterial wall rich in mycolic acid (waxy)
Acid-fast cells stay red; others take methylene blue

short.a: Mycobacteria have a waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acid that does not take up ordinary stains. Strong carbol fuchsin is heated until steam rises so the dye penetrates the wall. Once stained, the cells resist decolourisation by acid (20% sulphuric acid or acid-alcohol), hence 'acid-fast'. They appear red, while non-acid-fast cells lose colour and take the methylene blue counterstain (blue). Heat fixing first sticks the smear to the slide and kills organisms.

short.q: Why can a Gram-positive organism appear Gram-negative? (Gram variability)
short.hi: पुरानी culture या ज़्यादा decolourisation से Gram +ve भी pink दिखता है

kp.t: Old cultures with damaged cell wall
Use fresh 18-24 h cultures and controls

short.a: Gram variability means a Gram-positive organism stains partly or fully pink. Causes: over-decolourisation with alcohol or acetone, old (stationary/decline phase) cultures whose peptidoglycan wall is damaged by autolysis, cells treated with cell-wall antibiotics like penicillin, and thick or thin smears. Some organisms (e.g. Actinomyces, some Bacillus) are naturally variable. Fresh 18-24 hour cultures, correct timing and known positive and negative controls avoid wrong results.

short.q: Define D-value and Z-value. Why are they important?
short.hi: D-value = 90% microbes मारने का समय; Z-value = D-value को 10 गुना बदलने वाला temperature

kp.t: D-value: time to reduce population by 90% (1 log)
Z-value: temperature change to change D by 10 times
Used to design and validate sterilization cycles

short.a: D-value (decimal reduction time) is the time in minutes at a stated temperature required to kill 90% of the microbial population (one log reduction). Z-value is the rise in temperature (°C) needed to reduce the D-value by a factor of 10. For Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores, D121 is about 1.5-2 minutes and z about 10°C. These values describe the heat resistance of organisms and are used to design, compare and validate sterilization cycles and to calculate F-values.

short.q: Why does dry heat sterilization need a higher temperature and longer time than moist heat?
short.hi: Dry heat oxidation से मारता है, steam की latent heat से moist heat जल्दी काम करता है

kp.t: Moist heat kills by coagulation/denaturation of proteins
Steam gives latent heat on condensation, better penetration

short.a: Moist heat (steam) kills microbes by coagulation and denaturation of proteins, which occurs at lower temperature when water is present; steam also releases a large latent heat on condensation and penetrates rapidly. Dry heat kills by oxidation of cell constituents and transfers heat slowly (air is a poor conductor). Hence autoclaving needs 121°C for 15 min, while a hot air oven needs about 160°C for 2 hours (or 170°C for 1 h, 180°C for 30 min).

short.q: Why is filtration used for heat-sensitive solutions, and what is its limitation?
short.hi: 0.22 µm filter bacteria रोकता है पर virus और mycoplasma निकल सकते हैं

kp.t: Needs aseptic filling and integrity test

short.a: Filtration physically removes microorganisms without heat, so it is used for heat-sensitive solutions such as protein drugs, serum, vaccines, some antibiotics and ophthalmic solutions. A sterilizing-grade membrane of 0.22 µm pore size retains bacteria. Limitations: viruses, mycoplasma and endotoxins may pass; filters can clog or break; the filtrate must be filled aseptically; and filter integrity must be checked (bubble point test) before and after use.

short.q: Why is removal of air important in an autoclave? Name one test for it.
short.hi: Air रहने पर temperature 121°C तक नहीं पहुँचता — Bowie-Dick test

kp.t: Air-steam mixture has lower temperature than pure steam at same pressure
Air pockets block steam penetration (cold spots)

short.a: Sterilization depends on saturated steam at 121°C (15 psi). If air remains, the steam-air mixture has a lower temperature than pure steam at the same pressure, and trapped air pockets in porous loads prevent steam contact, creating cold spots where microbes survive. Air is removed by downward (gravity) displacement or pre-vacuum pulses. The Bowie-Dick test (a test pack with heat-sensitive indicator sheet) checks air removal and steam penetration in porous-load autoclaves.

short.q: Name the biological indicator organisms used for different sterilization methods.
short.hi: Steam के लिए Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores

kp.t: Dry heat: Bacillus atrophaeus (B. subtilis var. niger)

short.a:
Biological indicators are standardized preparations of highly resistant bacterial spores:
- Moist heat (steam): Geobacillus stearothermophilus.
- Dry heat: Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly B. subtilis var. niger).
- Ethylene oxide: Bacillus atrophaeus.
- Ionizing radiation: Bacillus pumilus.
- Filtration: Brevundimonas diminuta (challenge organism for 0.22 µm filters).
After the cycle the indicator is incubated; no growth shows that the cycle was lethal.

short.q: Give the principle of radiation sterilization and one pharmaceutical application.
short.hi: Gamma rays (Cobalt-60) DNA तोड़कर microbes मारती हैं

kp.t: Ionizing radiation: gamma rays from Cobalt-60 / electron beam
Cold sterilization of disposables (syringes, sutures, gloves)

short.a: Ionizing radiation (gamma rays from Cobalt-60, or high-energy electron beams) ionizes molecules and produces free radicals that break microbial DNA, killing cells without heating ('cold sterilization'). A dose of 25 kGy is the usual standard. It is used for prepacked disposable plastic syringes, needles, catheters, surgical gloves, sutures and some heat-sensitive powders. Non-ionizing UV light (about 260 nm) acts on DNA (thymine dimers) but penetrates poorly, so it is used only for air and surfaces.

short.q: What is F0 value? State its significance.
short.hi: F0 = 121°C पर product को मिला equivalent sterilizing time

kp.t: Sums lethality over whole heating and cooling cycle
Used to validate/compare steam cycles (overkill F0 ≥ 12)

short.a: F0 value is the equivalent time in minutes at 121°C delivered to a product by a moist heat sterilization cycle, calculated assuming a z-value of 10°C. It adds up the lethal effect of all temperatures during heating, holding and cooling. It allows cycles at different temperatures to be compared, helps reduce heat damage to products, and is used in validation; an overkill cycle usually aims at F0 of 12 minutes or more, while a standard 15 min at 121°C gives F0 about 15.

short.q: Interpret Gram staining results obtained from a mixed culture.
short.hi: Mixed culture में purple (Gram +ve) और pink (Gram -ve) दोनों दिखेंगे

kp.t: Principle: thick peptidoglycan retains crystal violet-iodine complex
Steps: crystal violet, iodine, alcohol/acetone, safranin
Report shape and arrangement of each type
Check controls / Gram variability; subculture to isolate

a.intro: Gram staining divides bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative based on cell wall structure. In a mixed culture both types (and different shapes) are seen in the same smear, and the result must be read and reported for each population.
points: Principle and steps: crystal violet (primary stain, 1 min), Gram's iodine (mordant, 1 min), decolourise with alcohol or acetone (few seconds), counterstain with safranin (30-60 s). Gram-positive cells keep the crystal violet-iodine complex in their thick peptidoglycan; Gram-negative cells lose it as the lipid outer membrane dissolves and take safranin.
Reading: Gram-positive cells appear purple/violet and Gram-negative cells appear pink/red under oil immersion (100x).

Report each population by colour, shape and arrangement, e.g. 'Gram-positive cocci in clusters (suggests Staphylococcus) and Gram-negative rods (suggests Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli)'; note relative numbers.

Pitfalls: over-decolourisation makes Gram-positive look negative; under-decolourisation makes Gram-negative look positive; old cultures, thick smears and antibiotic-treated cells cause Gram variability; always run known controls (S. aureus and E. coli).

Next steps: Gram stain is only presumptive; streak on selective/differential media (mannitol salt agar, MacConkey) to obtain pure cultures, then confirm by biochemical tests (catalase, coagulase, IMViC).
a.diagram: Draw a circle (microscope field) with purple grape-like clusters of cocci and pink short rods scattered; label 'Gram +ve cocci (purple)' and 'Gram -ve bacilli (pink)'.
a.conclusion: Correct interpretation of a mixed Gram stain tells which groups of contaminants are present and guides selective isolation and identification.

short.q: Discuss operational qualification of large-scale sterilization equipment.
short.hi: OQ = equipment सही तरीके से specification के अनुसार चलता है, यह साबित करना

kp.t: Part of validation: DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ
OQ: equipment works within set limits (empty chamber)
Heat distribution study with thermocouples / cold spot
Alarms, interlocks, vacuum leak test, Bowie-Dick
Equipment: large autoclaves, dry heat tunnels, EtO chambers, irradiators

a.intro: Large-scale sterilization equipment (production autoclaves, dry heat ovens and depyrogenation tunnels, ethylene oxide chambers, gamma irradiators, filtration systems) must be validated. Qualification is done in steps: design (DQ), installation (IQ), operational (OQ) and performance (PQ). OQ proves that the installed equipment operates as intended throughout its specified operating ranges.
points: Pre-requisites: approved protocol, completed IQ (utilities like clean steam, power, drains connected as designed), calibrated instruments.
Calibration and function checks: temperature and pressure sensors, recorders, timers, door seals, safety valves, steam traps, fans (in tunnels) and conveyor speeds are verified against standards.
Controls and safety: test alarms, door interlocks, power-failure recovery, control software/sequence (vacuum pulses, heating, exposure, exhaust, drying).

Empty-chamber heat distribution: many thermocouples placed throughout the empty chamber in repeated runs to show uniform temperature (e.g. within about ±1°C of set point in autoclaves) and find the cold spot.

Steam autoclave specific tests: vacuum leak rate test, air removal (Bowie-Dick) test, steam quality (dryness, non-condensable gases, superheat). Tunnels: air velocity, HEPA integrity, particle counts. EtO: gas concentration, humidity and temperature control.

Acceptance and documentation: results compared with acceptance criteria, deviations investigated, report approved before PQ (loaded-chamber heat penetration studies with biological indicators) and routine use; requalification periodically and after changes.
a.diagram: Draw an autoclave chamber outline with numbered thermocouple points distributed at corners, centre and near drain, wires leading to a data logger; mark the 'cold spot' near the drain.
a.conclusion: OQ gives documented evidence that the sterilizer works within limits, forming the base for PQ and assuring the required SAL.

short.q: Explain the selection and interpretation of sterility indicators.
short.hi: Sterility indicators: physical, chemical और biological — process के अनुसार चुनें

kp.t: Chemical indicators: Browne's tubes, tapes, colour change
Select BI organism by method (stearothermophilus, atrophaeus, pumilus)
Place at cold spot / hardest-to-sterilize location
Interpretation: no growth = pass; growth = failure, investigate

a.intro: Sterility indicators are devices that show whether the conditions needed for sterilization were achieved in a cycle. They are of three types: physical, chemical and biological. The indicator chosen must match the sterilization method and be placed where conditions are worst.
points: Physical indicators: thermometers, thermocouples, pressure gauges, recorder charts, F0 calculation; they show the cycle parameters but not lethality inside every pack.

Chemical indicators: substances that change colour or melt at set conditions, e.g. Browne's tubes (red to green), autoclave tape (stripes darken), Bowie-Dick sheets, integrators, EtO and radiation-sensitive dots; quick to read but only show exposure, not microbial kill.

Biological indicators: standardized spore preparations (about 10^5-10^6 spores) of known resistance: Geobacillus stearothermophilus (steam), Bacillus atrophaeus (dry heat, EtO), Bacillus pumilus (radiation), Brevundimonas diminuta (filters).

Selection: match indicator to process and its key variables; know the D-value of the BI; place indicators at the cold spot, centre of dense packs and hardest-to-reach areas, along with positive (unexposed) controls.

Interpretation: physical and chemical indicators must meet set values; BIs are incubated in suitable medium (e.g. 55-60°C for G. stearothermophilus); no growth means the cycle achieved the required lethality; growth or wrong colour means cycle failure, the load is rejected or reprocessed and the cause investigated.
a.conclusion: Using all three indicator types together gives the best assurance; biological indicators are the most direct proof of lethality.

short.q: Describe sterilization by filtration. Add a note on membrane filters and filter integrity testing.
short.hi: Membrane filter (0.22 µm) microbes को रोककर sterile filtrate देता है

kp.t: Membrane filters of cellulose esters, nylon, PVDF, 0.22 µm
Depth filters: sintered glass, Seitz (asbestos) pads
For heat-labile liquids and gases (HEPA for air)
Integrity: bubble point / diffusion / pressure hold test
Limitations: viruses, mycoplasma pass; needs aseptic filling

a.intro: Filtration sterilizes liquids and gases by physically removing microorganisms rather than killing them. It is the method of choice for heat-sensitive solutions and is followed by aseptic filling.
points: Mechanism: microbes are retained by sieving (pores smaller than cells), adsorption to the filter matrix and entrapment in depth filters.
Depth filters: sintered glass, unglazed porcelain (Chamberland candles), Seitz asbestos pads; used as prefilters; may shed fibres.

Membrane (screen) filters: thin films of cellulose esters, nylon, PVDF, polysulfone, with uniform pores; 0.22 µm (or 0.2 µm) is sterilizing grade, 0.45 µm for clarification and microbial counts; low adsorption and no shedding.

Procedure: membrane in a holder is sterilized (autoclaved) beforehand; solution is passed under positive pressure or vacuum, often through a prefilter; filtrate is collected aseptically in sterile containers under laminar air flow.

Integrity testing: bubble point test (pressure at which gas bubbles first pass through a wetted membrane), diffusion (forward flow) test and pressure hold test, done before and after filtration; challenge validation with Brevundimonas diminuta.
Merits and demerits: no heat, fast, removes particles too; but cannot remove viruses and mycoplasma reliably, risk of filter failure and adsorption of drug, needs aseptic handling.
a.diagram: Draw a filter holder: inlet with pressure, prefilter disc, membrane on support screen, O-ring seal, outlet to a sterile receiver; label pore size 0.22 µm.
a.conclusion: Filtration with validated membranes and integrity tests is essential for sterile ophthalmic solutions, biological products and sterile air.

short.q: Classify fungi based on morphology with examples.
short.hi: Fungi: yeast, mould, yeast-like और dimorphic
short.a:
Morphologically fungi are:
1. Yeasts: unicellular, round/oval, reproduce by budding, e.g. Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Cryptococcus neoformans.
2. Moulds (filamentous): branched hyphae forming mycelium, e.g. Aspergillus, Penicillium, Mucor, Rhizopus.
3. Yeast-like fungi: buds that elongate into pseudohyphae, e.g. Candida albicans.
4. Dimorphic fungi: yeast form in tissue/37°C and mould form at 25°C, e.g. Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Sporothrix.

short.q: Write the methods used for cultivation of viruses.
short.hi: Virus केवल जीवित cells में उगते हैं: animal, egg, cell culture

kp.t: Viruses grow only in living cells (obligate intracellular)
Embryonated hen's egg (chorioallantoic membrane, amniotic, allantoic, yolk sac)
Cell / tissue culture, detected by cytopathic effect

short.a:
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites and cannot grow on artificial media. They are cultivated in:
1. Experimental animals, e.g. suckling mice.
2. Embryonated hen's eggs (8-11 days old) by inoculation into the chorioallantoic membrane (pocks), amniotic cavity, allantoic cavity (influenza vaccine) or yolk sac.
3. Cell (tissue) cultures: primary, diploid and continuous cell lines; growth seen as cytopathic effect (CPE), haemadsorption or interference.

short.q: Differentiate between antiseptic, disinfectant and sanitizer.
short.hi: Antiseptic जीवित tissue पर, disinfectant निर्जीव वस्तुओं पर

kp.t: Sanitizer: reduces microbes to safe public-health level

short.a:
Antiseptic: a chemical that destroys or inhibits microorganisms on living tissue (skin, wounds) without harming it, e.g. povidone iodine, chlorhexidine, 70% alcohol.
Disinfectant: a chemical that kills vegetative pathogens (not necessarily spores) on inanimate objects such as floors, instruments and equipment, e.g. phenol, hypochlorite, formaldehyde.
Sanitizer: an agent that reduces the microbial count on surfaces (e.g. food utensils) to a safe public-health level.

short.q: Give the mode of action of phenols and quaternary ammonium compounds.
short.hi: Phenol: protein denature; QAC: cell membrane damage

kp.t: Phenols: denature proteins, damage cell membrane
QACs inactivated by soaps/anionics and organic matter

short.a:
Phenols (phenol, cresols, chloroxylenol): at low concentration they damage the cytoplasmic membrane causing leakage of cell contents; at higher concentration they coagulate and denature proteins. They remain active in organic matter.
Quaternary ammonium compounds (benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide) are cationic surface-active agents; they adsorb to the negatively charged cell surface, disrupt the cytoplasmic membrane, cause leakage and denature proteins. They are inactivated by soaps (anionic), hard water and organic matter, and do not kill spores.

short.q: Name the culture media and incubation conditions used in the sterility test (IP).
short.hi: FTM (bacteria, 30-35°C) और SCDM (fungi, 20-25°C), 14 दिन

kp.t: Fluid thioglycollate medium for anaerobes and aerobes
Soybean casein digest medium for fungi and aerobes

short.a:
Pharmacopoeial sterility test (IP/BP/USP harmonised) uses two media:
1. Fluid thioglycollate medium (FTM): mainly for anaerobic and also aerobic bacteria; incubated at 30-35°C.
2. Soybean-casein digest medium (SCDM / tryptone soya broth): for fungi and aerobic bacteria; incubated at 20-25°C.
Both are incubated for not less than 14 days and observed for turbidity. Media are checked for sterility and growth promotion before use.

short.q: What is method suitability (validation) in sterility testing? Why is it needed?
short.hi: Product की antimicrobial activity test को false negative न कर दे, यह जाँच

kp.t: Checks product does not inhibit microbial growth
Inoculate not more than 100 CFU of test organisms
Test organisms: S. aureus, B. subtilis, P. aeruginosa, C. sporogenes, C. albicans, A. brasiliensis
Prevents false negative; use neutraliser/dilution/membrane rinse

short.a: Method suitability (formerly bacteriostasis and fungistasis test) confirms that the product itself does not inhibit microbial growth under test conditions. Media containing the product (or the rinsed membrane) are inoculated with not more than 100 CFU of S. aureus, B. subtilis, P. aeruginosa, Clostridium sporogenes, Candida albicans and Aspergillus brasiliensis. Growth must be comparable to the control. If inhibited, the antimicrobial is neutralised, diluted or removed by membrane rinsing. It prevents false negative (falsely 'sterile') results.

short.q: Explain the evaluation of disinfectants using the phenol coefficient method.
short.hi: Phenol coefficient = disinfectant की तुलना phenol से (Rideal-Walker / Chick-Martin)

kp.t: PC = dilution of test killing in 7.5 min but not 5 min ÷ same for phenol
Limitations: only for phenolics, one organism, no organic load (RW)

a.intro: The phenol coefficient compares the bactericidal activity of a disinfectant with that of phenol under identical conditions. A value above 1 means the disinfectant is more effective than phenol.
points: Rideal-Walker (RW) test: a series of dilutions of test disinfectant and of phenol are prepared; 5 mL of each is inoculated with 0.2 mL of a 24 h broth culture of Salmonella typhi at 17-18°C.
At 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 minutes a loopful from each tube is transferred to nutrient broth, incubated at 37°C for 48-72 h and observed for growth.
Calculation: RW coefficient = dilution of disinfectant that kills in 7.5 min but not in 5 min ÷ dilution of phenol that does the same.
Chick-Martin test: disinfectant acts for 30 min in the presence of organic matter (dried yeast or faeces) on S. typhi (and S. aureus); more realistic for use conditions.

Limitations: valid mainly for phenolic disinfectants; one organism; RW has no organic load; results depend on strain, medium and temperature; does not show sporicidal or virucidal activity. Use-dilution (Kelsey-Sykes, AOAC) and capacity tests are better alternatives.
a.diagram: Draw a table/grid: rows = dilutions (e.g. 1:100, 1:110, 1:120) of test and phenol; columns = 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 min; mark + (growth) and - (no growth); circle the dilution giving + at 5 min and - at 7.5 min.
a.conclusion: Phenol coefficient is a simple screening comparison; practical use-dilution tests are needed to choose in-use concentrations.

short.q: Discuss the factors influencing disinfection.
short.hi: Concentration, time, temperature, pH, organic matter, microbe का प्रकार

kp.t: Type and number of microbes (spores, mycobacteria resistant)

a.intro: The activity of a disinfectant is not fixed; it depends on the agent, the organism and the environment. Understanding these factors helps choose the right agent and in-use concentration.
points: Concentration: activity rises with concentration; the concentration exponent (n) shows how strongly dilution reduces activity (phenol n = 6, so halving concentration cuts activity 64-fold; for mercurials n is about 1).
Time of contact: killing follows an approximately logarithmic (first-order) death rate; enough contact time is essential.
Temperature: activity increases with temperature, expressed as temperature coefficient (Q10).
pH: affects ionization of agent and cell surface; phenols and acids work better at acidic pH, QACs and glutaraldehyde at alkaline pH.
Organic matter: blood, pus, serum, faeces react with or protect microbes and inactivate halogens and QACs; surfaces should be cleaned first.
Type, number and state of organisms: spores > mycobacteria > non-enveloped viruses > fungi > vegetative bacteria > enveloped viruses in resistance; larger populations and biofilms need longer time.
Others: interfering substances (hard water, soaps for QACs), formulation and surface type.
a.conclusion: Effective disinfection needs the right agent, correct concentration, adequate time, suitable pH and temperature, and clean surfaces.

short.q: Explain the evaluation of bacteriostatic and bactericidal activity of antimicrobial agents.
short.hi: Bacteriostatic: growth रोकता (MIC); bactericidal: मारता (MBC)

kp.t: MBC by subculturing clear tubes (99.9% kill)
Agar diffusion / cup plate / disc zone of inhibition

a.intro: A bacteriostatic agent inhibits multiplication (growth resumes when it is removed), whereas a bactericidal agent kills the organisms. Evaluation tells the potency and type of action.
points: Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC): serial two-fold dilutions of the agent in broth are inoculated with a standard inoculum (about 10^5-10^6 CFU/mL) and incubated; the lowest concentration with no visible turbidity is the MIC.
Agar diffusion: cup-plate or disc method; zone of inhibition indicates inhibitory activity; agar dilution plates can also give MIC.
Minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC): samples from clear MIC tubes are subcultured onto agar free of agent (with neutraliser); the lowest concentration killing 99.9% of the inoculum is the MBC.
Interpretation: if MBC is close to MIC (MBC/MIC ratio about 4 or less) the agent is bactericidal; a much higher MBC suggests bacteriostatic action.

Time-kill (viable count) method: organisms exposed to the agent; samples taken at intervals, neutralised and plated; a fall of 3 log (99.9%) shows bactericidal action, while static agents keep counts near the starting level.
a.diagram: Draw a row of tubes with decreasing concentration: turbid tubes at low concentration, clear tubes at higher; mark the first clear tube 'MIC', then arrows from clear tubes to agar plates showing growth or no growth, marking 'MBC'.
a.conclusion: MIC and MBC testing differentiates static from cidal action and guides dosing and preservative selection.

short.q: Describe the replication of viruses with reference to the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage.
short.hi: Virus replication: attachment → penetration → uncoating → synthesis → assembly → release

kp.t: Penetration / injection of nucleic acid; uncoating
Eclipse phase: synthesis of viral nucleic acid and proteins
Lysogeny: prophage integrates in host DNA

a.intro: Viruses multiply only inside living host cells using the host's machinery. The T-even bacteriophage lytic cycle is the classic model; animal viruses follow similar steps.
points: Adsorption: tail fibres of the phage bind to specific receptors on the bacterial cell wall (host specificity).
Penetration: the tail sheath contracts and the phage DNA is injected; the empty capsid stays outside. Animal viruses enter by endocytosis or membrane fusion and then uncoat.
Eclipse phase (biosynthesis): no infectious virus is detectable; early proteins shut off host synthesis; viral nucleic acid is replicated and late (structural) proteins are made.
Assembly and maturation: capsid proteins assemble around nucleic acid to form new virions.
Release: phage lysozyme lyses the cell, releasing about 100-200 phages (burst size); enveloped animal viruses bud through the host membrane, gaining their envelope.
Lysogenic cycle: temperate phages (e.g. lambda) integrate DNA into the host chromosome as prophage, replicating with the host until induced to enter the lytic cycle.
a.diagram: Draw a sequence of 5 bacterial cells: (1) phage attached by tail fibres, (2) DNA injection, (3) phage DNA and protein parts inside, (4) assembled phages inside, (5) cell bursting releasing phages.
a.conclusion: Understanding replication explains viral cultivation, antiviral drug targets and vaccine production.

short.q: Why is aseptic processing preferred over terminal sterilization for protein formulations?
short.hi: Protein heat/radiation से denature होते हैं, इसलिए filtration + aseptic filling

kp.t: Proteins are heat-labile; denature/aggregate on heating
So sterile filtration (0.22 µm) + aseptic filling

short.a: Protein drugs (insulin, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, enzymes) are heat-labile: autoclaving denatures and aggregates them, causing loss of potency and possible immunogenicity. Radiation creates free radicals that oxidise and fragment proteins, and ethylene oxide alkylates them and leaves residues. Therefore they are sterilized by 0.22 µm membrane filtration and filled under aseptic processing (Grade A), even though terminal sterilization gives a higher SAL.

short.q: What are bioaerosols? Give their significance in a cleanroom.
short.hi: Bioaerosol = हवा में तैरते microbes वाले कण

kp.t: Sources: personnel (skin flakes, breath), HVAC, materials
Can settle on open products → contamination
Monitored by settle plates / active air samplers

short.a: Bioaerosols are airborne particles (about 0.5-100 µm) that contain or carry living microorganisms, their spores or fragments. In a cleanroom they arise mainly from personnel (skin flakes, coughing, talking), poor HVAC, open doors and materials. They can settle on exposed sterile products and surfaces, so they are a main contamination risk in aseptic filling. They are controlled by HEPA filtration and gowning and monitored with settle plates and active air samplers (CFU/m3).

short.q: What is the role of unidirectional airflow in aseptic processing?
short.hi: Unidirectional (laminar) airflow कणों को critical zone से दूर बहा देता है

kp.t: HEPA-filtered air moving in parallel streams at uniform velocity
Sweeps particles away from critical zone

short.a: Unidirectional (laminar) airflow supplies HEPA-filtered air in parallel streams at a uniform velocity (about 0.36-0.54 m/s, EU GMP guidance). It continuously sweeps particles and microbes away from the critical zone where sterile product, containers and closures are exposed, preventing their settling and avoiding turbulence. It provides Grade A (ISO 5) conditions for aseptic filling, sterility testing and other open manipulations.

short.q: What is a HEPA filter? State its efficiency.
short.hi: HEPA filter 0.3 µm कणों को 99.97% रोकता है

kp.t: Integrity tested by DOP/PAO aerosol test

short.a: A HEPA (High Efficiency Particulate Air) filter is a pleated mat of glass (borosilicate) microfibres separated by spacers. It removes at least 99.97% of particles of 0.3 µm diameter (the most penetrating particle size) by interception, impaction and diffusion, and therefore retains bacteria and spores. It is used in laminar flow units and cleanroom air supply, and its integrity is checked by DOP/PAO aerosol challenge tests.

short.q: Give the classification of clean areas as per EU GMP / WHO with ISO equivalents.
short.hi: Grade A (ISO 5) सबसे साफ़; Grade D सबसे कम

kp.t: Grade B: background for Grade A
Grade C and D: less critical stages
Based on particle counts (≥0.5 µm per m3), at rest and in operation

short.a:
Clean areas are graded by airborne particles and microbes:
- Grade A: high-risk operations (filling, open sterile handling) under unidirectional airflow; ISO 5 (Class 100), max 3,520 particles ≥0.5 µm/m3.
- Grade B: background room for Grade A aseptic work; ISO 5 at rest, ISO 7 in operation.
- Grade C: less critical steps (e.g. preparing solutions to be filtered); ISO 7 at rest.
- Grade D: handling of components after washing; ISO 8 at rest.
Limits apply 'at rest' and 'in operation'.

short.q: State the principle of microbiological assay.
short.hi: Microbiological assay: test organism की growth पर inhibition/response को standard से compare करना

kp.t: Potency measured by biological response of a test organism
Inhibition of growth (antibiotics) or growth promotion (vitamins)
Compared with a reference standard of known potency

short.a: Microbiological assay determines the potency (biological activity) of a substance by measuring its effect on a sensitive test microorganism under standard conditions and comparing it with a reference standard of known potency. Antibiotics inhibit growth (zone of inhibition or reduced turbidity); vitamins and amino acids promote growth of organisms that need them. Within a range, the response is proportional to the logarithm of the dose, allowing calculation of potency.

short.q: Why are microbiological assays used for antibiotics and vitamins instead of only chemical assays?
short.hi: Microbial assay असली biological activity बताता है

kp.t: Detects loss of activity / degradation that chemical assays miss
Useful for complex mixtures (e.g. gentamicin, polymyxin, neomycin)
Highly sensitive, small quantities (vitamin B12 in ng)

short.a: Chemical assays measure the amount of molecule, but microbiological assays measure the real biological activity. They detect small changes in activity (e.g. degradation products that are inactive but chemically similar), are suitable for antibiotics that are mixtures of related components (gentamicin, neomycin, polymyxin B, bacitracin) and for which no simple chemical method exists, and are very sensitive, detecting vitamins like B12 at nanogram levels. Hence IP/BP prescribe them for many antibiotics.

short.q: Differentiate between the cylinder-plate (cup-plate) method and the turbidimetric (tube) method of antibiotic assay.
short.hi: Cup-plate: zone diameter; turbidimetric: broth की turbidity

kp.t: Cup-plate: diffusion through agar, zone of inhibition
Turbidimetric: growth in liquid broth measured as turbidity/absorbance
Turbidimetric faster (3-4 h incubation) vs plate 16-18 h
Test organisms e.g. B. subtilis / S. aureus (plate), S. aureus / E. coli (tube)
Turbidimetric not for coloured/turbid samples; plate is simple

a.intro: Both are official (IP) methods for determining antibiotic potency against a reference standard, but they measure different responses.
points: Principle: cylinder-plate measures diffusion of antibiotic through seeded agar giving a circular zone of inhibition; turbidimetric measures inhibition of growth in a liquid medium as reduced turbidity.

Procedure: plate method uses agar seeded with test organism, cylinders or cups filled with standard and test dilutions, incubated about 16-18 h at 32-37°C, zone diameters measured; tube method adds dilutions to broth inoculated with organism, incubated 3-4 h, growth stopped (formaldehyde) and absorbance read at about 530 nm.
Response: zone diameter is proportional to log concentration; turbidity (absorbance) decreases with log concentration.
Merits of plate: simple, cheap, many samples on one plate, unaffected by sample colour or turbidity. Demerits: longer incubation, zone affected by diffusion rate, agar depth, pre-incubation.
Merits of turbidimetric: rapid, more precise, not affected by diffusion. Demerits: sample must be clear and colourless, sensitive to temperature and timing, needs spectrophotometer.
Examples: plate for streptomycin, neomycin, bacitracin; turbidimetric for tetracyclines, gentamicin, streptomycin (as per IP tables).
a.diagram: Draw a Petri plate with 4-6 cylinders on seeded agar and clear zones of different sizes around them (S = standard, T = test). Beside it, a row of tubes with decreasing turbidity as concentration increases.
a.conclusion: The plate method is the common routine choice, while the turbidimetric method is preferred where speed and precision are required.

short.q: Explain the working of laminar airflow equipment. Differentiate horizontal and vertical laminar flow cabinets.
short.hi: Laminar flow: fan → prefilter → HEPA → parallel साफ़ हवा work area पर

kp.t: Blower draws room air through prefilter
HEPA filter gives particle-free air in parallel streams
Vertical: air flows down onto work surface
UV lamp, velocity check, routine testing

a.intro: Laminar airflow (LAF) equipment provides a Grade A (ISO 5) work zone by supplying HEPA-filtered air in uniform parallel streams. It is used for aseptic manipulations, sterility testing and media preparation.
points: Construction: cabinet with stainless steel work surface, blower (fan), prefilter, plenum, HEPA filter, side panels/glass sash, UV lamp, fluorescent light, pressure gauge (manometer).

Working: blower draws room air through the prefilter (removes coarse dust) into the plenum; it is forced through the HEPA filter; clean air flows at about 0.45 m/s over the work area, sweeping particles away.
Horizontal LAF: HEPA filter at the back; air flows horizontally towards the operator; good product protection; not for hazardous materials because air blows on the operator.
Vertical LAF: HEPA filter in the roof; air flows downward onto the work surface and exits through front/bottom; less turbulence from objects; gives some operator protection.
Biological safety cabinets (Class II) are vertical-flow cabinets that also exhaust air through HEPA, protecting operator, product and environment; used for pathogens, cytotoxics and cell culture.
Maintenance: UV on before use, surfaces wiped with 70% alcohol, air velocity checked by anemometer, HEPA integrity by DOP/PAO test, particle counts and settle plates.
a.diagram: Draw a horizontal LAF: box with blower at the bottom back, prefilter, HEPA filter on the back wall, arrows of parallel air moving horizontally across the work table to the front. Draw a vertical LAF with HEPA in the roof and arrows going down.
a.conclusion: LAF equipment is the heart of aseptic work; its choice (horizontal, vertical or biosafety cabinet) depends on whether product, operator or both need protection.

short.q: Why can preservative failure occur in multidose formulations?
short.hi: Multidose में बार-बार खोलने से contamination; preservative कम असर कर सकता है

kp.t: Partitioning into oil phase / sorption to container or rubber
Wrong pH (e.g. benzoic acid needs acidic pH) or degradation

short.a: Multidose products are opened repeatedly, introducing microorganisms each time. The preservative may fail because its free (active) concentration falls: binding to non-ionic surfactants (polysorbate micelles) or polymers, partitioning into the oil phase of emulsions, sorption into rubber closures or plastic containers, chemical degradation or volatilisation, and unsuitable pH (weak acids like benzoic/sorbic acid work only in unionised form at acidic pH). Resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa or a heavy inoculum can also overcome it.

short.q: Why is mycoplasma contamination difficult to detect in cell cultures?
short.hi: Mycoplasma बहुत छोटे, cell wall नहीं, culture साफ़ दिखती है

kp.t: Very small (0.2-0.3 µm), pass 0.22 µm filters
No cell wall: not seen by Gram stain, resistant to penicillin
No turbidity or visible change in culture
Detected by PCR, DNA (Hoechst) staining, culture

short.a: Mycoplasmas are the smallest free-living bacteria (about 0.2-0.3 µm) and lack a cell wall. They do not make the medium turbid or cause obvious cytopathic effect, they cannot be seen under an ordinary light microscope or by Gram stain, they can pass through 0.22 µm filters and they are resistant to penicillin and other cell-wall antibiotics used in media. So contamination stays hidden while it alters cell metabolism; special tests (PCR, Hoechst/DAPI DNA staining, broth-agar culture) are needed.

short.q: Mention any one industrial application of mammalian cell culture.
short.hi: Mammalian cell culture से vaccines और monoclonal antibodies बनते हैं
short.a: Mammalian cell cultures are used industrially to produce viral vaccines (e.g. polio and rabies vaccines in Vero cells or human diploid cells) and recombinant therapeutic proteins such as monoclonal antibodies, erythropoietin and tissue plasminogen activator in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells or hybridomas. Mammalian cells perform correct folding and glycosylation, which bacteria cannot. They are also used for cytotoxicity testing and drug screening.

short.q: What are the types of microbial spoilage? Give the signs of spoilage in pharmaceutical products.
short.hi: Spoilage: physical, chemical, biological — रंग, गंध, gas, turbidity बदलना

kp.t: Physical changes: turbidity, sedimentation, emulsion cracking, viscosity change
Chemical: pH change, drug degradation, gas formation
Organoleptic: off odour, taste, colour change

short.a:
Microbial spoilage is deterioration of a product caused by microbial growth or metabolism.
Types/signs:
- Physical: turbidity in solutions, cracking/phase separation of emulsions, change in viscosity, sedimentation, caking.
- Chemical: pH change, breakdown of drug and excipients (sugars, surfactants), gas formation (fermentation).
- Organoleptic: unpleasant odour, taste, discolouration.
- Visible growth: mould colonies, slime, pellicle.
- Health hazard: infection (especially in eye drops, injections), toxins and pyrogens, loss of potency.

short.q: List the ideal properties of a preservative used in pharmaceutical products.
short.hi: Ideal preservative: broad spectrum, कम मात्रा में असरदार, non-toxic, stable

kp.t: Compatible and stable over pH range and shelf life
Colourless, odourless, tasteless; not lost to container

short.a: An ideal preservative should be: broad spectrum (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) and preferably microbicidal; effective at low concentration; quick acting; non-toxic, non-irritant and non-sensitizing at use levels; chemically and physically stable over the product's pH range and shelf life; compatible with drug, excipients and container (not adsorbed or lost by partitioning); soluble enough in the aqueous phase; colourless, odourless and tasteless; and economical. Examples: parabens, benzalkonium chloride, benzyl alcohol, chlorocresol, sorbic acid.

short.q: What are the sources of microbial contamination of pharmaceutical products?
short.hi: Contamination के sources: water, raw materials, personnel, air, equipment, packaging

kp.t: Raw materials, especially natural origin (starch, gelatin, gums)

short.a:
Main sources:
1. Water: largest raw material; carries Gram-negative bacteria like Pseudomonas, coliforms.
2. Raw materials: natural products (starch, gelatin, gums, talc, herbal drugs) carry spores and moulds.
3. Personnel: skin and hair flora (Staphylococcus aureus), respiratory droplets, faecal organisms from poor hygiene.
4. Air and environment: dust, mould spores, Bacillus spores.
5. Equipment and buildings: poorly cleaned machines, pipes, drains with biofilm.
6. Packaging: containers and closures.
7. In-use contamination by the patient (fingers, droppers).

short.q: Discuss the factors affecting microbial spoilage of semisolid formulations.
short.hi: Creams/ointments में water activity, pH, preservative, packaging spoilage तय करते हैं

kp.t: Water activity / water content (o/w creams more prone)
Preservative partitioning into oil / binding to emulsifier
Packaging: tubes vs jars; repeated finger contact
Storage temperature and initial contamination load

a.intro: Semisolids (creams, gels, ointments) often contain water and nutrients and are applied with fingers, so they are prone to spoilage by Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, yeasts and moulds. The extent of spoilage depends on formulation, packaging and use.
points: Water activity: microbes need available water; anhydrous ointments (petrolatum) resist growth, while o/w creams and aqueous gels with high water activity spoil easily; high sugar or glycerol lowers water activity.
Nutritional content: natural gums, starches, gelatin, proteins, some surfactants and oils can be metabolised as carbon and nitrogen sources.
pH and redox potential: near-neutral pH suits most bacteria, acidic pH favours fungi; emulsions with entrapped air allow aerobes.

Preservative availability: preservatives partition into the oil phase or bind to non-ionic emulsifiers (polysorbates) and polymers, lowering free aqueous concentration; pH may ionise weak acid preservatives.
Packaging and use: open jars allow repeated finger contact and air contamination; collapsible tubes with small orifices reduce contamination; some preservatives are absorbed by plastic containers.
Storage and initial bioburden: warm, humid storage increases growth; contaminated water or raw materials and poor hygiene raise starting numbers.
a.conclusion: Spoilage of semisolids is controlled by low water activity where possible, effective preservative systems that remain available, good manufacturing hygiene and protective packaging such as tubes.

short.q: Explain the assessment of microbial load and particulate burden in non-sterile products.
short.hi: Non-sterile products में TAMC, TYMC और specified organisms की जाँच

kp.t: Total combined yeast and mould count (TYMC)
Methods: plate count, membrane filtration, MPN
Tests for specified organisms (E. coli, Salmonella, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus)
Acceptance limits per dosage form (e.g. oral 10^3 TAMC)
Particulate burden: visual inspection, light obscuration, microscopy

a.intro: Non-sterile products (tablets, syrups, creams) need not be sterile but must have a low microbial count and be free from specified objectionable organisms. Pharmacopoeias (IP, BP, USP) give microbial enumeration tests and tests for specified microorganisms, with limits for each dosage form.
points: Sample preparation: product dissolved or suspended in buffered sodium chloride-peptone solution (pH 7.0), with neutralisers (lecithin, polysorbate 80) for preservatives; method suitability checked with test strains.
Total aerobic microbial count (TAMC): soybean-casein digest agar, 30-35°C, 3-5 days; by pour plate, spread plate, membrane filtration or MPN; result in CFU per g or mL.
Total combined yeasts and moulds count (TYMC): Sabouraud dextrose agar, 20-25°C, 5-7 days.

Specified organisms: enrichment and selective media to show absence of E. coli (oral products), Salmonella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus (topical and nasal), bile-tolerant Gram-negatives, Candida albicans (vaginal), Clostridia.
Acceptance criteria: e.g. non-aqueous oral preparations TAMC 10^3 and TYMC 10^2 CFU/g; aqueous oral 10^2 and 10^1 CFU/mL; cutaneous 10^2 and 10^1 CFU/g or mL (harmonised pharmacopoeial table).

Particulate burden: visible particles checked by visual inspection against black and white backgrounds; sub-visible particles by light obscuration counters or microscopic count (mainly for liquids and inhalations); raw materials and water also monitored (bioburden, endotoxin) to control overall load.
a.conclusion: Regular enumeration, specified-organism tests and particulate checks keep non-sterile products within safe limits and detect contamination early.

short.q: Differentiate between primary, established (continuous) and transformed cell cultures.
short.hi: Primary: सीधे tissue से; established: लगातार चलने वाली cell line; transformed: cancer जैसे गुण

kp.t: Primary culture: directly from tissue, limited life
Finite cell lines/diploid strains: about 50 divisions (Hayflick limit)
Established/continuous lines: unlimited divisions (HeLa, Vero, CHO)
Transformed: altered by virus/chemicals, loss of contact inhibition

a.intro: Animal cell cultures are grouped according to their origin and life span in culture.
points: Primary culture: cells taken directly from an animal tissue (e.g. monkey kidney, chick embryo fibroblasts) by mechanical or enzymatic (trypsin) disaggregation; retain normal characteristics; heterogeneous; limited life; needed fresh each time.

Secondary/finite cell lines (diploid cell strains): obtained by subculturing primary cultures; normal diploid karyotype; divide only a limited number of times (about 50, the Hayflick limit), e.g. WI-38 and MRC-5 human lung fibroblasts used for vaccines.

Established (continuous) cell lines: cells that have become immortal and can be subcultured indefinitely, e.g. HeLa, Vero, CHO, BHK-21; often aneuploid; grow faster and to higher density; easy to maintain.

Transformed cells: cells whose growth properties have changed spontaneously or by viruses (SV40), chemicals or radiation; show loss of contact inhibition, anchorage-independent growth (in soft agar), reduced serum need, and may form tumours in animals.

Uses: primary cells for virus isolation and research on normal physiology; diploid strains for human vaccines; continuous lines for large-scale production of vaccines and recombinant proteins, though their products need tests for residual DNA and adventitious agents.
a.conclusion: The choice of culture type balances normal behaviour (primary, diploid) against ease of large-scale growth (continuous lines).

long.q: Describe the ultrastructure of a bacterial cell with a neat labelled diagram.
long.hi: Bacterial cell: cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, flagella, pili, capsule

a.intro: A bacterial cell is a prokaryotic cell of about 1-10 µm. Its structures are grouped as external (capsule, flagella, pili), cell envelope (cell wall, cytoplasmic membrane) and internal (cytoplasm, ribosomes, nucleoid, inclusions, spores).
points: Capsule/slime layer: polysaccharide or polypeptide layer outside the wall; protects from phagocytosis and drying; a virulence factor (e.g. Pneumococcus).
Flagella: long thin protein (flagellin) appendages for motility; arrangements monotrichous, lophotrichous, amphitrichous, peritrichous.
Pili/fimbriae: short hair-like protein structures for attachment; sex pili transfer DNA in conjugation.
Cell wall: rigid peptidoglycan layer giving shape and protection from osmotic lysis; thick with teichoic acid in Gram-positive; thin with outer LPS membrane in Gram-negative.
Cytoplasmic membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins; selective permeability, transport, respiration enzymes (bacteria lack mitochondria).
Mesosomes: infoldings of the membrane, thought to help in respiration and cell division.
Cytoplasm: aqueous gel containing enzymes, nutrients and 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) for protein synthesis.
Nucleoid: single circular double-stranded DNA without nuclear membrane; plasmids are small extra-chromosomal DNA carrying genes like drug resistance.
Inclusion bodies: storage granules such as volutin (metachromatic granules), glycogen, poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate.
Endospores: highly resistant dormant structures formed by Bacillus and Clostridium; resist heat and disinfectants, hence important in sterilization.
a.diagram: Draw an oval/rod cell. Label from outside in: capsule, cell wall, cytoplasmic membrane, mesosome (infolding), cytoplasm with ribosomes (dots), nucleoid (coiled DNA), plasmid (small ring), inclusion granules, flagellum (long whip at one end), pili (short hairs on surface).
a.conclusion: Knowing bacterial structure explains Gram staining, antibiotic targets (cell wall, ribosomes) and resistance of spores to sterilization.

long.q: Explain the bacterial growth curve in detail. Add a note on factors affecting growth and methods of measuring bacterial growth.
long.hi: Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, decline; measure by total और viable count

a.intro: Bacteria multiply by binary fission. When a small inoculum is put into a fresh liquid medium in a closed (batch) system and log of the number of viable cells is plotted against time, a characteristic growth curve is obtained.
points: Lag phase: cells adjust to the new medium, synthesize enzymes and increase in size; little or no increase in number.

Log (exponential) phase: cells divide at a constant maximum rate; generation (doubling) time is shortest and constant (about 20 min for E. coli in ideal conditions); cells are uniform and most sensitive to antibiotics.

Stationary phase: nutrients are used up and toxic metabolites accumulate; rate of cell division equals rate of death, so viable count stays constant; secondary metabolites (antibiotics, exotoxins) and spores are produced.
Decline (death) phase: death rate exceeds division; viable count falls exponentially; involution forms appear.
Generation time: g = t / n, where n (number of generations) = (log N - log N0) / log 2.
Factors affecting growth: nutrients, temperature, pH, oxygen, osmotic pressure, moisture, CO2, light and presence of inhibitors.
Total count methods: direct microscopic count (Petroff-Hausser chamber), Coulter counter, turbidity/optical density, dry weight, total nitrogen.
Viable count methods: serial dilution followed by pour plate or spread plate count (CFU/mL), membrane filter count and MPN method.
a.diagram: Graph with X-axis 'time (hours)' and Y-axis 'log number of viable cells'. A flat start (lag), a straight steep rising line (log), a flat top plateau (stationary) and a falling line (decline). Label each phase.
a.conclusion: The growth curve guides harvesting of cells or antibiotics in fermentation and explains why young (log phase) cultures are used in sensitivity tests and assays.

long.q: Describe the principle, working and applications of phase contrast microscopy and dark field microscopy.
long.hi: Phase contrast: बिना stain के जीवित cells देखना; dark field: काली background पर चमकते cells

kp.t: Phase contrast: converts phase difference into brightness difference
Dark field: only scattered light enters objective
Dark field condenser with central stop
Dark field use: spirochaetes like Treponema

a.intro: Ordinary bright field microscopes give little contrast for unstained, transparent cells. Phase contrast and dark field microscopes create contrast without staining, so living organisms and their motility can be studied.
points: Phase contrast principle: light passing through a cell is slowed (phase shifted, about 1/4 wavelength) compared with light passing through the medium; the microscope converts these invisible phase differences into visible differences of brightness.

Phase contrast construction: an annular diaphragm (ring) in the condenser gives a hollow cone of light; a phase plate (phase ring) in the objective advances or retards direct light so it interferes with diffracted light.
Phase contrast image: cell structures appear dark on a bright background (positive phase contrast); internal structures like nucleus, granules and spores become visible.
Phase contrast uses: observing living unstained cells, motility, cell division, spores, cell culture monitoring, protozoa.

Dark field principle: the specimen is lit by oblique light that does not enter the objective directly; only light scattered by the object enters, so the object shines bright against a dark background.
Dark field construction: an ordinary microscope fitted with a dark field condenser having a central opaque stop (disc), which blocks central rays and gives a hollow cone of light.
Dark field uses: very thin organisms below resolution of bright field, e.g. Treponema pallidum (syphilis), Leptospira, Borrelia; motility studies.
Limitations: dark field gives no internal detail; dust gives artefacts; phase contrast shows halos around objects.
a.diagram: Phase contrast: draw light source, annular diaphragm (ring) below condenser, hollow cone of light, specimen, objective with phase plate (ring), eyepiece. Dark field: light source, condenser with central black stop, oblique rays crossing the specimen, only scattered rays entering the objective; result a bright cell on black field.
a.conclusion: Both microscopes allow study of live, unstained microbes; dark field is the classic method for diagnosing spirochaetes.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction and applications of electron microscopy. Differentiate between TEM and SEM.
long.hi: Electron microscope में light की जगह electron beam, बहुत ज़्यादा resolution

kp.t: Uses beam of electrons instead of light
Very short wavelength gives high resolution / magnification
TEM: electrons pass through ultrathin section, internal detail
Specimen staining with heavy metals (osmium, uranyl, gold coating)

a.intro: The resolving power of a microscope depends on the wavelength used. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, so the electron microscope resolves objects down to about 0.1-1 nm, far beyond the light microscope (about 0.2 µm). It is used to see viruses and ultrastructure of cells.
points: Principle: a beam of electrons from a heated tungsten filament is accelerated by high voltage and focused by electromagnetic lenses on the specimen; the image is formed by electrons that pass through or are scattered from the specimen.

Construction: electron gun (cathode filament, anode), condenser electromagnetic lens, specimen chamber, objective and projector lenses, fluorescent screen or camera; the whole column is under high vacuum because air scatters electrons.

Specimen preparation: fixation (glutaraldehyde, osmium tetroxide), dehydration, embedding in resin, ultrathin sectioning by ultramicrotome, staining with heavy metals (uranyl acetate, lead citrate); negative staining (phosphotungstic acid) for viruses; shadow casting, freeze fracture.
Transmission electron microscope (TEM): electrons pass through an ultrathin section; gives a 2D image of internal structure; very high resolution (about 0.1-0.5 nm).
Scanning electron microscope (SEM): a fine beam scans the surface of a metal (gold)-coated specimen; secondary electrons emitted are detected; gives a 3D image of surface; lower resolution than TEM.
Applications: study of viruses, bacterial ultrastructure (flagella, pili, ribosomes), cell organelles, surface of particles and tablets, biofilms.
Limitations: costly, specimens must be dead and dried under vacuum, artefacts possible, image is black and white.
a.diagram: Draw a vertical column: electron gun at top, condenser lens, specimen, objective lens, projector lens, fluorescent screen at bottom, with a note 'vacuum pump' attached. For SEM add scanning coils and a detector beside the specimen.
a.conclusion: Electron microscopy made viruses and cell ultrastructure visible and is essential in microbiology research and pharmaceutical particle analysis.

long.q: What are culture media? Classify them. Describe the isolation of pure cultures and the cultivation of anaerobes.
long.hi: Media के प्रकार + pure culture isolation + anaerobic culture

a.intro: Culture media are nutrient preparations used to grow, isolate, identify and maintain microorganisms in the laboratory. Most clinical bacteria grow as colonies on solid media, from which pure cultures are obtained.
points: Raw materials: peptone (nitrogen), meat/yeast extract (vitamins, minerals), carbohydrates, NaCl, agar (solidifying), blood/serum (enrichment), indicators, distilled water.
By consistency: liquid (broth), semisolid (0.5% agar, for motility), solid (1.5-2% agar).
By composition: synthetic/defined and complex (non-synthetic).

By function: basal (nutrient agar), enriched (blood, chocolate agar), enrichment (selenite F), selective (MacConkey, Lowenstein-Jensen), differential/indicator (MacConkey for lactose fermenters), transport (Stuart's), anaerobic (Robertson's cooked meat).
Isolation of pure culture: streak plate method, where the loop spreads the sample over successive areas so single cells give isolated colonies.
Pour plate and spread plate: serial dilutions mixed in molten agar or spread on the surface; isolated colonies are picked and subcultured.
Other isolation: enrichment culture, selective media, micromanipulator (single cell), animal inoculation.
Cultivation of anaerobes: reducing media with thioglycollate, cysteine, cooked meat; resazurin indicator.
Anaerobic jar (McIntosh and Fildes): air replaced by hydrogen; palladium catalyst converts remaining O2 to water; methylene blue indicator; Gas-Pak envelope generates H2 and CO2.
Others: anaerobic glove box/chamber, deep shake culture, alkaline pyrogallol (Buchner's) method.
a.diagram: Draw a streak plate (Petri dish divided into 3-4 streak areas, isolated colonies in last area) and an anaerobic jar (metal jar with lid, gas inlet and outlet valves, catalyst capsule under lid, plates stacked inside, indicator tube).
a.conclusion: Proper media and techniques give pure cultures, which are essential for identification, sensitivity testing, assays and industrial fermentation.

long.q: Describe the principle, construction, working, merits, demerits and applications of moist heat sterilization by autoclave. How is its efficiency evaluated?
long.hi: Autoclave: 121°C, 15 psi, 15 min — saturated steam से protein coagulation

kp.t: Principle: saturated steam under pressure, protein coagulation
Construction: chamber, jacket, safety valve, pressure gauge, steam trap
Merits: rapid, reliable, kills spores, non-toxic
Demerits: not for oils, powders, heat-labile drugs
Evaluation: biological indicator G. stearothermophilus, thermocouples, Bowie-Dick

a.intro: Moist heat in the form of saturated steam under pressure is the most reliable and widely used method of sterilization. The autoclave is a pressure vessel that raises the boiling point of water so that steam at 121°C (15 psi above atmospheric) can be used.
points: Principle: saturated steam condenses on cooler articles, releasing latent heat and moisture; this coagulates and denatures microbial proteins and enzymes, killing vegetative cells and spores.
Cycles: 121°C for 15 min (15 psi), 115°C for 30 min, or 134°C for 3 min (high-vacuum autoclaves).

Construction: a stainless steel chamber (often jacketed), tight lid/door with gasket, steam supply or electric heater, pressure gauge, thermometer/temperature sensor in the drain, safety valve, air/steam release (vent) valve, steam trap and drain, perforated tray.

Working: water is heated, air is removed by downward displacement or vacuum pulses; once pure steam fills the chamber the vent is closed; pressure and temperature rise to 121°C; holding time is counted; then exhaust and drying (for porous loads) follow; pressure is released slowly to avoid boiling of liquids.
Large-scale types: gravity displacement autoclaves, pre-vacuum (porous load) autoclaves, and air-steam mixture/water spray autoclaves for sealed containers that need over-pressure.
Merits: rapid heating and penetration, kills spores, reliable and easy to control, no toxic residue, cheap.
Demerits: not suitable for oils, fats, powders (steam cannot penetrate), heat-sensitive drugs and some plastics; may corrode instruments; wet packs.
Applications: aqueous injections in sealed ampoules/vials, culture media, surgical dressings, rubber closures, glassware, instruments, waste decontamination.

Evaluation of efficiency: physical (thermocouples, temperature-time charts, pressure records), chemical indicators (Browne's tubes, autoclave tape, Bowie-Dick test for air removal) and biological indicators (Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore strips; no growth after incubation means sterilization).
Validation uses D-value, F0 value and bioburden to show SAL of 10^-6.
a.diagram: Draw a vertical (laboratory) autoclave: cylindrical chamber with water at the bottom and heating element, perforated tray holding articles, lid with clamps and gasket, pressure gauge, safety valve and air/steam vent valve on the lid, steam trap and drain at bottom, labelled arrows for steam flow.
a.conclusion: The autoclave is the method of choice for anything that can withstand moist heat, and its cycles are validated with physical, chemical and biological indicators.

long.q: Discuss gaseous and radiation methods of sterilization with principle, procedure, merits, demerits and applications.
long.hi: Gaseous: ethylene oxide, formaldehyde, H2O2 vapour; Radiation: gamma, UV

kp.t: EtO conditions: temperature, humidity, concentration, time
Gamma radiation from Cobalt-60, dose 25 kGy
UV radiation 260 nm, thymine dimers, poor penetration
Merits/demerits: EtO toxic & residues; radiation costly, may damage plastics

a.intro: Heat-sensitive materials such as plastics, rubber and some drugs cannot be autoclaved. They are sterilized by gases (chemical sterilants that act at low temperature) or by radiation (cold sterilization).
points: Ethylene oxide principle: alkylates -SH, -NH2, -OH and -COOH groups of proteins and nucleic acids, killing vegetative cells and spores.

Ethylene oxide procedure: articles in gas-permeable packs are pre-humidified (about 40-60% RH), exposed to EtO (about 400-1000 mg/L, often mixed with CO2) at about 50-60°C for several hours in a sealed chamber, then evacuated and aerated to remove residues.

EtO merits and demerits: penetrates packaging and plastics, good for heat-sensitive devices; but toxic, carcinogenic, flammable/explosive, slow, leaves residues needing aeration; biological indicator Bacillus atrophaeus.
