Formaldehyde: gas from formalin (heating or with KMnO4) used for fumigating rooms, aseptic areas and equipment; low-temperature steam with formaldehyde (LTSF) for heat-sensitive items; irritant, poor penetration, possible carcinogen.
Hydrogen peroxide vapour/gas plasma: oxidizing; used for isolators, rooms and medical devices; breaks down to water and oxygen (no toxic residue); not for cellulose or liquids.

Gamma radiation: Cobalt-60 source; ionization and free radicals break DNA; dose usually 25 kGy; deep penetration through final packs; used for disposable syringes, sutures, gloves, catheters; biological indicator Bacillus pumilus.
Electron beam: accelerated electrons; fast, but poorer penetration than gamma.

Radiation merits and demerits: no heat, terminal sterilization in final pack, continuous process, no residue; but costly plant, safety shielding needed, may discolour glass and degrade plastics and some drugs.
UV radiation: non-ionizing, about 260 nm, forms thymine dimers in DNA; poor penetration, so used only for air, surfaces, laminar flow cabinets and water.
a.diagram: Draw an EtO steriliser chamber: sealed chamber with gas inlet, vacuum pump, humidifier, heater jacket, exhaust to aeration. For gamma, draw a cobalt-60 source pool with shielding walls (concrete maze) and a conveyor carrying product boxes around the source.
a.conclusion: Gaseous and radiation methods extend sterilization to heat-sensitive products, but they need careful control of conditions and residue/safety checks.

long.q: Explain the principle and procedure of acid-fast staining and the IMViC tests. How do they help in the identification of bacteria?
long.hi: ZN stain mycobacteria के लिए; IMViC enteric bacteria पहचानने के लिए

kp.t: ZN steps: carbol fuchsin with heat, 20% H2SO4, methylene blue
Result: red bacilli on blue background
Methyl red test: mixed acid fermentation

a.intro: Bacteria are identified from their morphology and staining reactions followed by biochemical tests. Acid-fast staining identifies mycobacteria, while IMViC is a group of four tests used to differentiate members of Enterobacteriaceae, especially coliforms.
points: Acid-fast principle: mycobacteria contain mycolic acid in the wall; once stained with hot carbol fuchsin they resist decolourisation by acid.

Ziehl-Neelsen procedure: heat-fixed smear flooded with strong carbol fuchsin and heated till steam rises for about 5 min; washed; decolourised with 20% sulphuric acid (or acid-alcohol) until pale pink; washed; counterstained with methylene blue (or malachite green) for 1-2 min; washed, dried, examined under oil immersion.
Result: acid-fast bacilli red/pink; non-acid-fast cells and background blue. Uses: diagnosis of tuberculosis and leprosy; Kinyoun (cold) method is a variant.
Indole test: organism grown in tryptone/peptone water; tryptophanase converts tryptophan to indole; Kovac's reagent gives a red ring (positive, e.g. E. coli).
Methyl red test: glucose phosphate broth; mixed acid fermentation drops pH below about 4.4; methyl red turns red (positive, E. coli); yellow is negative.
Voges-Proskauer test: same broth; butanediol fermentation gives acetoin; with alpha-naphthol and KOH (Barritt's reagent) a pink-red colour appears (positive, Enterobacter, Klebsiella).
Citrate test: Simmons citrate agar; organisms using citrate as sole carbon source make the medium alkaline and bromothymol blue turns from green to blue (positive, Enterobacter, Klebsiella).
Interpretation: E. coli ++-- ; Enterobacter aerogenes/Klebsiella --++.
Importance: detecting E. coli (faecal indicator) in water, raw materials and products; identifying pathogens in clinical and quality control labs.
a.diagram: Draw a table: rows E. coli and Enterobacter; columns I, M, Vi, C; fill + + - - and - - + +. Optionally sketch a test tube with red ring on top (indole positive).
a.conclusion: Staining gives quick presumptive identification and IMViC confirms coliform type; together they guide quality control and diagnosis.

long.q: Describe the morphology, classification, reproduction and cultivation of fungi. Add a note on their pharmaceutical importance.
long.hi: Fungi: eukaryotic, chitin wall, hyphae; spores से प्रजनन; SDA पर culture

kp.t: Eukaryotic, chitin cell wall, ergosterol membrane

a.intro: Fungi are eukaryotic, non-photosynthetic, heterotrophic organisms with a rigid cell wall of chitin (and glucans) and ergosterol in their membrane. They include yeasts and moulds and are important both as producers of drugs and as contaminants of pharmaceuticals.
points: Morphology: moulds have long tubular hyphae (septate in Aspergillus, Penicillium; aseptate/coenocytic in Mucor, Rhizopus) forming mycelium (vegetative and aerial); yeasts are single oval cells.
Morphological classification: yeasts (Saccharomyces, Cryptococcus), yeast-like (Candida with pseudohyphae), filamentous moulds, dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma).

Taxonomic classification (by sexual spores): Zygomycetes (zygospores; Mucor, Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (ascospores in asci; Saccharomyces, Aspergillus, Penicillium have ascomycete states), Basidiomycetes (basidiospores; mushrooms, Cryptococcus), Deuteromycetes/Fungi imperfecti (no known sexual stage).
Asexual reproduction: budding (yeasts), fragmentation of hyphae, fission, and asexual spores such as conidia (Penicillium, Aspergillus), sporangiospores (Rhizopus), arthrospores, chlamydospores.
Sexual reproduction: fusion of compatible nuclei (plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis) forming zygospores, ascospores or basidiospores.

Cultivation: Sabouraud dextrose agar (pH about 5.6, low pH and high sugar suppress bacteria; chloramphenicol may be added), potato dextrose agar, Czapek-Dox medium; incubated at 20-25°C (or 37°C for pathogenic yeast phase) for several days; slide culture to study spore arrangement.
Identification: colony texture and colour, microscopy with lactophenol cotton blue mount, KOH mount, germ tube test for Candida.

Pharmaceutical importance: production of penicillin (Penicillium chrysogenum), griseofulvin, cephalosporin (Acremonium), citric acid (Aspergillus niger), enzymes, vitamins and steroid transformations; yeasts in fermentation; moulds spoil tablets, syrups and creams; pathogens cause mycoses (candidiasis, aspergillosis).
a.diagram: Draw Penicillium (septate conidiophore ending in brush-like phialides bearing chains of conidia), Aspergillus (conidiophore with swollen vesicle and radiating chains of conidia) and Rhizopus (aseptate hyphae, rhizoids, sporangiophore with round sporangium), and a budding yeast cell.
a.conclusion: Fungi are both valuable producers of medicines and a major cause of pharmaceutical spoilage, so their recognition and control are essential.

long.q: Describe the morphology, classification, replication and cultivation of viruses.
long.hi: Virus: nucleic acid (DNA या RNA) + capsid; केवल जीवित cells में बढ़ते हैं

kp.t: Acellular; DNA or RNA, never both
Capsid of capsomeres; envelope in some
Classification by nucleic acid, symmetry, envelope (Baltimore)
Replication steps: adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis, assembly, release

a.intro: Viruses are the smallest infectious agents (about 20-300 nm), acellular and obligate intracellular parasites. They contain only one type of nucleic acid and depend fully on host cells for replication, so they are not affected by antibacterial antibiotics.
points: Structure: nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA, single or double stranded) surrounded by a protein coat (capsid) made of capsomeres; capsid plus nucleic acid = nucleocapsid; some have a lipid envelope with glycoprotein spikes (e.g. influenza, HIV).
Symmetry/morphology: helical (tobacco mosaic virus, influenza nucleocapsid), icosahedral/cubical (adenovirus, poliovirus), complex (poxvirus, bacteriophage with head and tail).

Classification: by nucleic acid type (DNA/RNA, ss/ds), symmetry, presence of envelope, size and site of assembly; Baltimore classification groups viruses into seven classes by genome and mRNA synthesis route; also by host (animal, plant, bacterial viruses = bacteriophages).

Replication: adsorption to specific receptors, penetration (endocytosis, fusion, or injection by phages), uncoating, eclipse phase with synthesis of viral nucleic acid and proteins, assembly/maturation, and release by lysis or budding.
Lytic and lysogenic cycles in bacteriophages; latency in some animal viruses (herpes).
Cultivation in animals: suckling mice, guinea pigs, monkeys; used for pathogenicity and some vaccine work.
Cultivation in embryonated hen's eggs (8-11 days): chorioallantoic membrane (pox viruses, pocks), allantoic cavity (influenza for vaccines), amniotic cavity, yolk sac.

Cultivation in cell culture: primary cells (monkey kidney), diploid cell strains (WI-38, MRC-5), continuous cell lines (HeLa, Vero); detected by cytopathic effect, haemadsorption, interference, immunofluorescence.
Assay of viruses: plaque assay (PFU), haemagglutination, TCID50.
a.diagram: Draw an enveloped icosahedral virus: central nucleic acid, icosahedral capsid made of capsomeres, outer lipid envelope with spikes; label each. Also draw a T-even phage: polyhedral head with DNA, collar, tail sheath, base plate, tail fibres.
a.conclusion: Knowledge of viral structure and cultivation is the basis for vaccine production, antiviral drug testing and viral safety of biologicals.

long.q: Classify disinfectants and explain their mode of action. Discuss the factors influencing disinfection and the evaluation of antiseptics and disinfectants.
long.hi: Disinfectants: phenols, alcohols, halogens, aldehydes, QACs; evaluation: phenol coefficient, use-dilution

kp.t: Factors: concentration, time, temperature, pH, organic matter

a.intro: Disinfectants are chemical agents used to destroy pathogenic microorganisms on inanimate objects; antiseptics are applied to living tissues. They differ in spectrum, speed and mode of action, and must be evaluated before use.
points: Phenolics: phenol, cresols, chloroxylenol, hexachlorophene; membrane damage and protein denaturation; active in organic matter.
Alcohols: ethanol and isopropanol at 60-90% (70% optimal); denature proteins and dissolve lipids; not sporicidal; skin antisepsis.
Halogens: chlorine compounds (sodium hypochlorite, chloramines) and iodine (tincture, povidone iodine); oxidize -SH groups and halogenate proteins; broad spectrum.
Aldehydes: formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde (2%, alkaline); alkylate amino, carboxyl and sulfhydryl groups; sporicidal (high-level disinfectants, 'cold sterilants').
Surface-active agents: QACs (benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide) disrupt membranes; inactivated by soaps; biguanides (chlorhexidine) damage membranes.
Others: oxidizing agents (hydrogen peroxide, peracetic acid), heavy metals (mercurials, silver nitrate) combining with -SH groups, dyes (crystal violet, acriflavine), acids and alkalis.

Factors influencing disinfection: concentration (concentration exponent), contact time, temperature (Q10), pH, organic load, type and number of organisms, presence of biofilm and interfering substances.

Evaluation: phenol coefficient tests (Rideal-Walker with S. typhi; Chick-Martin with organic matter), use-dilution test (stainless steel carriers), Kelsey-Sykes capacity test (repeated challenge with organic soil), in-use test (sampling used disinfectant), suspension and surface tests; antiseptics tested on skin (bacterial count before and after) and for irritancy.
a.conclusion: Choosing a disinfectant depends on its class, mode of action and evaluated activity under real use conditions; rotation and correct dilution prevent resistance and failure.

long.q: Discuss the sterility testing of pharmaceutical products as per IP/BP/USP. Describe membrane filtration and direct inoculation methods.
long.hi: Sterility test: membrane filtration या direct inoculation; FTM और SCDM, 14 दिन

kp.t: Test for presence of viable microbes in sterile products
Done under aseptic conditions (Grade A / isolator)
Membrane filtration: 0.45 µm, rinse, transfer membrane
Number of containers / quantities as per pharmacopoeia
Method suitability, growth promotion and negative controls
Interpretation and retest only if test invalid

a.intro: The sterility test detects viable microorganisms in products that are labelled sterile (injections, ophthalmic preparations, sterile powders, devices). The IP, BP (Ph. Eur.) and USP tests are harmonised. Because only a sample is tested, a pass shows only that no contamination was found under test conditions; sterility is assured by validated manufacture.
points: Environment: performed in a Grade A laminar air flow within a Grade B room, or in an isolator; operators gowned; negative controls to check aseptic technique.

Culture media: fluid thioglycollate medium (anaerobes and aerobes, 30-35°C) and soybean-casein digest medium (fungi and aerobes, 20-25°C); each batch checked for sterility and growth promotion (S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, C. sporogenes, B. subtilis, C. albicans, A. brasiliensis).

Method suitability: test repeated with not more than 100 CFU of each organism added in presence of product to show no inhibition; inhibitory products need neutralisation, dilution or membrane rinsing.

Number of items: depends on batch size (e.g. for parenterals, 10% or 4 containers for batches up to 100, 10 containers for 101-500, 2% or 20 containers for larger batches, as per pharmacopoeial tables); quantity per medium depends on container volume.

Membrane filtration (preferred for filterable aqueous, alcoholic or oily products, and antibiotics): contents filtered through a 0.45 µm membrane in a closed canister system; membrane rinsed with sterile fluid (e.g. peptone water) to remove antimicrobial residues; membrane (or halves) transferred to the two media or media added to canisters.

Direct inoculation: specified volume of product transferred directly into media (product volume not more than 10% of medium volume); used for non-filterable products like suspensions, ointments (dispersed with suitable agent), devices (immersed).
Solids: dissolved in a suitable sterile diluent then filtered, or added directly; ophthalmic ointments dissolved in sterile isopropyl myristate and filtered; ophthalmic solutions filtered.
Incubation and reading: not less than 14 days; examined periodically for turbidity; if product makes media turbid, subculture after 14 days for 4 more days.
Interpretation: no growth = complies; growth = does not comply, unless the test is proved invalid (failure of environment monitoring, media or technique), in which case it is repeated.
a.diagram: Draw a closed membrane filtration system: product container, peristaltic pump, tubing to two canisters each with a 0.45 µm membrane at the base, vents with filters; one canister filled with FTM, other with SCDM, labelled incubation temperatures.
a.conclusion: Sterility testing as per pharmacopoeia is a final quality check, but real sterility assurance comes from validated sterilization and aseptic processing.

long.q: Design an aseptic area for sterile injectables, justifying the layout, air handling and contamination control measures.
long.hi: Aseptic area: grades A-D, airlocks, pressure cascade, HEPA, gowning, smooth surfaces

kp.t: Zoning by grades A/B/C/D (black, grey, white areas)
Positive pressure cascade 10-15 Pa between grades
HEPA filtered air, high air changes, unidirectional flow at filling
Smooth, impervious, coved surfaces; no ledges
Pass boxes / interlocked doors; personnel and material flow separated

a.intro: An aseptic area is a specially designed clean room suite where sterile products, which cannot be terminally sterilized or are filled after sterilization, are handled with minimum risk of microbial and particulate contamination. The design aims to keep contamination out, remove what is generated, and prevent its accumulation.
points: Zoning and layout: areas arranged from least clean to most clean. Unclassified/black area (warehouse, washing), Grade D (component washing, solution preparation), Grade C (preparation of solutions to be filtered), Grade B background room containing Grade A filling zone under unidirectional airflow. Justification: each step is protected by a cleaner surrounding zone.

Personnel entry: through a series of change rooms (street clothes off, hand washing, sterile gowning, step-over bench) and airlocks, each a step cleaner; gowning reduces shedding, the biggest source of contamination.
Material entry: through pass boxes (with UV or dynamic HEPA), double-door autoclaves or depyrogenation tunnels opening directly into the clean side; interlocked doors so both cannot open at once.

Air handling: HEPA-filtered air supply with high air change rate (often 20 or more per hour for Grade C/D and much more for B); unidirectional flow (about 0.45 m/s) over critical zones; low-level return air grilles; RABS or isolators for highest protection.

Pressure cascade: cleanest room at highest pressure, with about 10-15 Pa difference between adjacent grades, so air always flows from clean to less clean areas; monitored by magnehelic gauges with alarms.
Environment: temperature about 20-24°C and relative humidity about 45-55% for operator comfort (less sweating and shedding) and product stability.

Construction finishes: smooth, hard, impervious, non-shedding surfaces (epoxy floors, coated panels), coved corners, flush lights and windows, no ledges, sinks or drains in Grade A/B, sealed ceilings; minimum equipment and furniture of stainless steel.
Flow: one-way flow of personnel, materials and waste to avoid cross-over; separate exit routes.
Cleaning and disinfection: written schedules, rotation of disinfectants plus a sporicide, fumigation (formaldehyde or H2O2 vapour) after shutdown.

Environmental monitoring: non-viable particle counts, settle plates, active air sampling, contact (RODAC) plates and glove prints, with alert and action limits; media fills to validate aseptic processing.
a.diagram: Draw a floor plan: corridor → change room 1 (Grade D) → change room 2 (Grade C) → gowning/airlock (Grade B) → aseptic filling room (Grade B) containing a box marked 'Grade A LAF / filling line'. Show pass box and double-door autoclave on one wall, arrows for personnel and material flow, and '+' signs increasing (e.g. +15, +30, +45 Pa) towards the filling room.
a.conclusion: A well-designed aseptic area combines zoning, pressure cascade, HEPA air, proper finishes, gowning and monitoring, so that sterility of injectables is built in, not just tested.

long.q: Discuss the sources of contamination in an aseptic area and the methods of their prevention.
long.hi: Contamination sources: personnel, air, water, raw materials, equipment, packaging

kp.t: Personnel: skin flakes, hair, breath, clothing — largest source
Cleaning, disinfection, sterilization of materials, monitoring

a.intro: Even a well-built aseptic area can be contaminated if microbes enter or grow inside it. Identifying each source and controlling it is the basis of aseptic processing.
points: Personnel: the largest source; humans shed millions of skin particles per minute carrying Staphylococcus, Micrococcus and other skin flora; talking, coughing and poor technique spread droplets.
Air: unfiltered or turbulent air carries dust, mould spores and bacteria; leakage through doors and faulty HEPA filters.
Water: used for washing and making solutions; can carry Pseudomonas and other Gram-negative bacteria and endotoxins; stagnant pipes form biofilms.
Raw materials: natural products (starch, gums, talc) carry spores and moulds; contaminated active ingredients.
Packaging components: containers, closures, tubing improperly washed or sterilized.
Equipment and building: surfaces, crevices, drains, cardboard, wooden items, poorly cleaned machines.
Prevention for personnel: selection, health checks, training in aseptic technique, hand washing, full sterile gowning (hood, mask, goggles, gloves, boots), minimum number of people, slow movement.
Prevention for air: HEPA-filtered supply, positive pressure cascade, airlocks, unidirectional airflow at critical points, isolators/RABS.

Prevention for water and materials: Water for Injection systems kept hot or circulating, sanitised; sterilization of components (autoclave, dry heat tunnel), filtration of solutions, wiping and pass-box transfer.

Surfaces and monitoring: validated cleaning and disinfectant rotation, fumigation, environmental monitoring (settle plates, air samplers, contact plates) with trend analysis, and media fill (process simulation) tests.
a.diagram: Draw a simple diagram with the aseptic room in the centre and arrows from six boxes: personnel, air, water, raw materials, packaging, equipment; under each arrow write the control measure (gowning, HEPA, WFI, testing, sterilization, cleaning).
a.conclusion: Contamination control is a system: good design, trained people, sterile materials and continuous monitoring together keep the aseptic area under control.

long.q: Explain the principles and methods of microbiological assay of antibiotics. Describe the cylinder-plate method with calculation of potency.
long.hi: Antibiotic assay: cylinder-plate (zone) और turbidimetric; standard से तुलना

kp.t: Principle: compare inhibition by test vs reference standard
Cylinders filled with standard and test dilutions
Potency calculation from log-dose response lines

a.intro: Microbiological assay of antibiotics measures their potency by comparing the inhibition of a sensitive test organism produced by the sample with that produced by a reference standard of known potency (in units or µg per mg). It measures true biological activity and is official in IP/BP/USP.
points: Principle: within a suitable range, the response (zone diameter or turbidity) is linearly related to the logarithm of the antibiotic concentration; parallel log dose-response lines of standard and test allow potency calculation.

Requirements: reference standard, specified test organism (e.g. Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, Micrococcus luteus, Bacillus pumilus, depending on antibiotic), media, phosphate buffers of stated pH, controlled temperature.

Cylinder-plate procedure: base layer of agar poured in plates; seed layer inoculated with standardized organism suspension poured over it; stainless steel cylinders (or cups bored, 'cup-plate') placed; filled with standard and test solutions at high and low dose (e.g. ratio 4:1 or 2:1).
Pre-diffusion (optional) and incubation at about 30-37°C for 16-18 h; zone diameters measured with a zone reader or vernier caliper.

Assay designs: 2+2 (two doses each of standard and test), 3+3 design, or standard curve (five-point) method with a reference concentration on each plate; replicated and randomised (Latin square) to reduce plate errors.

Calculation (2+2 design): from mean zones of standard high (SH), standard low (SL), test high (TH), test low (TL), log potency ratio M = [(TH + TL) - (SH + SL)] / [(TH - TL) + (SH - SL)] × log I, where I is the ratio between doses; potency = assumed potency × antilog M. Validity requires linearity and parallelism.
Turbidimetric method: dilutions in broth inoculated with organism (e.g. S. aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella), incubated 3-4 h, absorbance read; quicker and more precise but needs clear samples.
Factors affecting: inoculum size, agar depth and uniformity, pH, diffusion time, temperature, cylinder filling volume.
a.diagram: Draw a Petri plate (top view) with 4 or 6 cylinders alternately labelled SH, SL, TH, TL and clear circular zones of different sizes around them; also draw a graph of zone diameter (Y) against log dose (X) with two parallel straight lines for standard and test.
a.conclusion: With proper design and statistical validity checks, microbiological assay gives the true potency of antibiotics and is required for batch release of many products.

long.q: Describe the methods for standardization of vitamins and amino acids by microbiological assay. Add a note on the assessment of a new antibiotic.
long.hi: Vitamin/amino acid assay में auxotroph (Lactobacillus) की growth; new antibiotic का spectrum, MIC, toxicity

kp.t: Principle: growth of organism needing the vitamin/amino acid (auxotroph)
Basal medium lacking only the test nutrient
Examples: B12 (L. leichmannii), niacin (L. plantarum), riboflavin, calcium pantothenate

a.intro: Vitamins and amino acids are assayed microbiologically using organisms that cannot synthesize them and therefore grow in proportion to the amount supplied. A new antibiotic must be assessed in stages from laboratory activity to clinical use.
points: Principle: in a basal medium containing all nutrients except the one being assayed, growth of the test organism (turbidity or acid production) is proportional to the concentration of that vitamin or amino acid within a range.

Test organisms: mostly lactic acid bacteria (and some yeasts/moulds) that need the nutrient, e.g. Lactobacillus leichmannii for vitamin B12, L. plantarum for niacin and calcium pantothenate, L. casei (L. rhamnosus) for riboflavin and folic acid; Leuconostoc mesenteroides and Pediococcus for amino acids.

Procedure: standard and test solutions in graded volumes are added to tubes of basal medium, sterilized, inoculated with a washed suspension of the organism and incubated (about 37°C, 16-24 h for turbidity or up to 72 h for titration).
Measurement: turbidimetric (absorbance) or titrimetric (lactic acid produced titrated with 0.1 M NaOH); a standard curve of response vs concentration gives the test content.
Merits: very sensitive (nanogram levels for B12), specific for active forms; demerits: slow, needs careful control of contamination and conditions.

Assessment of a new antibiotic - laboratory: antimicrobial spectrum against many standard and clinical strains; MIC and MBC; bactericidal or bacteriostatic action (time-kill curves); effect of pH, serum and inoculum; development of resistance on repeated subculture; mode of action.

Assessment - preclinical: activity in infected animals (protective dose, ED50), acute and chronic toxicity (LD50), pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, half-life, excretion), stability and assay method.
Assessment - clinical: phase I (safety in volunteers), phase II and III (efficacy and dosage in patients), phase IV (post-marketing surveillance).
a.diagram: Draw a graph of response (turbidity or mL NaOH) on Y-axis against concentration of vitamin on X-axis showing a rising straight line (standard curve) with a test reading interpolated.
a.conclusion: Microbiological assays standardize vitamins and amino acids accurately, and a staged assessment ensures a new antibiotic is effective and safe before clinical use.

long.q: A solid dosage manufacturing area reports recurrent fungal contamination. Discuss the probable sources, investigation and corrective and preventive measures.
long.hi: Fungal contamination: humidity, raw materials (starch), HVAC, packaging — investigation + CAPA

kp.t: Sources: high humidity / condensation / water leaks
Natural raw materials (starch, talc, gums, herbal)
HVAC: dirty filters, ducts, poor air changes
Investigation: environmental monitoring, identify isolates (SDA), trend
CAPA: control RH, repair HVAC/HEPA, sporicidal disinfectant rotation
Test raw materials/products for TYMC, water activity, packaging

a.intro: Fungal contamination in a tablet or capsule area is usually caused by moulds such as Aspergillus, Penicillium, Cladosporium and Rhizopus, whose spores are airborne, resist drying and grow wherever moisture and organic matter are available. Recurrence means a continuing source has not been removed, so a structured investigation and CAPA are needed.
points: Probable source - environment: high relative humidity, condensation on cold surfaces, water leaks, damp walls and ceilings behind equipment, wet cleaning that does not dry.
Probable source - HVAC: clogged or wet prefilters and filters, mould in ducts, cooling coils and drain pans, inadequate air changes or pressure differentials allowing outside air in.
Probable source - materials: natural raw materials (maize starch, talc, lactose, gums, herbal powders), purified water used in granulation, cardboard and wooden pallets brought into production.
Probable source - process and people: slow or incomplete drying of granules (high moisture content), poor cleaning of dryers, granulators and dust collectors, personnel moving between areas.

Investigation: review environmental monitoring data and trends (settle plates, air samples, swabs on Sabouraud dextrose agar); identify the isolates to genus/species; map positive locations; check HVAC records, RH logs, cleaning records, raw material and water test results (TYMC) and finished product microbial limits; root cause analysis (fishbone, 5-why).
Product impact: test affected batches for TYMC and specified organisms, water activity and moisture; assess risk and decide release, rework or rejection.

Corrective actions: repair leaks; clean and disinfect HVAC ducts and replace filters; deep clean the area; use sporicidal agents (hypochlorite, hydrogen peroxide/peracetic acid) in rotation with routine disinfectants; fumigate if justified; remove cardboard and wood (de-boxing outside, plastic pallets).

Preventive actions: control RH (dehumidifiers, often below about 50-55%), maintain pressure cascade, validate drying end-point (LOD), test incoming natural raw materials for microbial limits, improve gowning and training, revise cleaning SOPs, increase monitoring frequency with alert and action limits, and verify effectiveness by trending.
a.diagram: Draw a fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram with 'Recurrent fungal contamination' at the head and bones labelled Environment (humidity, leaks), HVAC (filters, ducts), Materials (starch, water, cardboard), Methods (drying, cleaning), Personnel (gowning), Equipment (dryers, dust collector).
a.conclusion: Recurrent fungal contamination is controlled only when the root cause, usually moisture plus a spore source, is removed and monitoring shows a sustained return to normal levels.

long.q: Describe the general procedure for growth and maintenance of animal cells in culture. Discuss the challenges in scale-up.
long.hi: Cell culture: tissue → trypsin → medium + serum → 37°C, 5% CO2 → subculture; scale-up में shear, oxygen, contamination

kp.t: Cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen with DMSO
Challenges: shear, oxygen transfer, contamination, cost, lactate/ammonia

a.intro: Animal cell culture is the growth of cells taken from animal tissues in vitro under controlled conditions. It requires strict asepsis, complex media and a carefully controlled physical environment, and it becomes more difficult when moved from flasks to industrial bioreactors.
points: Laboratory set-up: Class II biosafety cabinet, CO2 incubator, inverted microscope, centrifuge, water bath, liquid nitrogen storage; all work done aseptically with sterile plasticware.

Isolation (primary culture): tissue is minced and disaggregated mechanically or with enzymes (trypsin, collagenase); cells washed and counted (haemocytometer, trypan blue for viability) and seeded into flasks.

Media: balanced salt solution base with glucose, amino acids, vitamins (e.g. MEM, DMEM, RPMI 1640), supplemented with 5-10% fetal bovine serum (growth factors, attachment factors) or serum-free defined supplements; antibiotics (penicillin-streptomycin) optional; phenol red as pH indicator.
Physical conditions: 37°C, humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2 to maintain bicarbonate-buffered pH about 7.2-7.4; correct osmolality (about 280-320 mOsm/kg).

Growth and maintenance: adherent cells attach and spread to form a monolayer; medium changed every 2-3 days; at confluence cells are detached with trypsin-EDTA and subcultured (passaged) at a lower density; suspension cells are diluted with fresh medium.
Quality control: regular checks for morphology, viability, mycoplasma, bacterial/fungal contamination, cross-contamination (cell line authentication).
Preservation: cells frozen slowly (about 1°C/min) in medium with 5-10% DMSO or glycerol and stored in liquid nitrogen (-196°C); master and working cell banks.

Scale-up systems: roller bottles, multilayer flasks, microcarrier beads (Cytodex) for anchorage-dependent cells, stirred-tank and airlift bioreactors (fed-batch or perfusion) for suspension-adapted cells like CHO.

Scale-up challenges: cells lack a cell wall and are damaged by shear from impellers and bubble bursting; oxygen transfer is limited (low solubility); accumulation of lactate and ammonia; pH and CO2 gradients; slow growth and long runs increase contamination risk (bacteria, mycoplasma, viruses); expensive media and serum batch variation; maintaining product quality (glycosylation) and genetic stability; strict regulatory validation.
a.diagram: Draw a T-flask with a monolayer of cells, an arrow showing trypsinisation to new flasks (subculture), and a stirred-tank bioreactor with labelled impeller, sparger (air/O2), pH and DO probes, medium feed and harvest lines.
a.conclusion: With strict asepsis, controlled environment and well-designed bioreactors, animal cell culture can be scaled up to produce vaccines and biologics reliably.

long.q: Discuss the types of microbial spoilage, factors affecting spoilage, sources of contaminants and assessment of microbial contamination and spoilage of pharmaceutical products.
long.hi: Spoilage के types, factors, sources और assessment

kp.t: Signs: turbidity, odour, gas, emulsion cracking, mould
Factors: water activity, pH, nutrients, temperature
Factors: redox, packaging, preservative, inoculum size
Sources: water, raw materials, personnel, air, equipment, packaging
Typical spoilers: Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, yeasts, moulds
Assessment: microbial limit tests (TAMC, TYMC, specified organisms)
Assessment of spoilage: physical/chemical tests, challenge test

a.intro: Microbial spoilage is the undesirable change in a pharmaceutical product caused by microorganisms or their metabolites. It can make the product unacceptable, ineffective or harmful, especially in sterile, ophthalmic and multidose products.
points: Types of spoilage: (a) physical/organoleptic - turbidity, colour change, off odours and tastes, gas, cracking of emulsions, loss of viscosity of gums, visible mould; (b) chemical - degradation of drug (e.g. penicillinase, steroid metabolism), excipients (sugars, surfactants, oils) and preservatives; (c) health hazard - infection (Pseudomonas in eye drops causing corneal damage), toxins and pyrogens.
Factors - water activity: growth needs available water; dry powders and tablets resist; syrups with high sugar have low water activity.
Factors - nutrients, pH and redox: natural ingredients supply nutrients; bacteria prefer near-neutral pH, fungi acidic; aerobic or anaerobic conditions select organisms.
Factors - temperature and storage: warm storage speeds growth; refrigeration slows it.
Factors - formulation and packaging: preservative type and availability, emulsion type (o/w more prone), container design (jars vs tubes, single vs multidose), inoculum size and type.

Sources of contaminants: water (Pseudomonas and other Gram-negatives), raw materials of natural origin (spores, moulds, Salmonella in gelatin), personnel (Staphylococcus aureus), air (mould spores, Bacillus), equipment and building, packaging and in-use contamination by patients.

Assessment of contamination: microbial enumeration (TAMC, TYMC) by plate count, membrane filtration or MPN; tests for specified organisms (E. coli, Salmonella, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, C. albicans); sterility test and bacterial endotoxin test for sterile products; environmental and water monitoring.

Assessment of spoilage: periodic physical (appearance, viscosity, pH, phase separation), chemical (assay of drug and preservative) and microbiological testing on stability; preservative efficacy (challenge) test; rapid methods (ATP bioluminescence, impedance).
a.diagram: Draw a flow chart: Sources (water, raw material, personnel, air, equipment, packaging) → Product → Growth (influenced by water activity, pH, temperature, nutrients, preservative) → Spoilage (physical, chemical, health hazard) → Assessment (microbial limits, challenge test, stability testing).
a.conclusion: Spoilage is prevented by controlling sources, designing hostile formulations with effective preservatives, proper packaging and regular microbial assessment.

long.q: Explain the preservation of pharmaceutical products using antimicrobial agents. Describe the evaluation of microbial stability of formulations (preservative efficacy test).
long.hi: Preservatives: parabens, benzalkonium, benzoic acid; challenge test से efficacy जाँचना

kp.t: Classes: acids (benzoic, sorbic), parabens, alcohols, phenols, QACs, mercurials
Factors: pH, partitioning, binding, container interactions
Organisms: S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, E. coli, C. albicans, A. brasiliensis
Sampling at intervals (0, 6 h, 24 h, 7, 14, 28 days)
Log reduction criteria and no increase

a.intro: Preservatives are antimicrobial agents added to non-sterile and multidose products to prevent growth of microorganisms introduced during manufacture or use. Their activity in the final formulation must be proved by the preservative efficacy (challenge) test.
points: Need for preservation: aqueous oral liquids, creams, multidose injections, eye drops and nasal sprays; not a substitute for good manufacturing practice.
Weak acids: benzoic acid and sodium benzoate, sorbic acid and potassium sorbate; active in unionised form, so used at acidic pH (below about 5).
Parabens (methyl, propyl, butyl p-hydroxybenzoates): broad spectrum, often combined (methyl + propyl) for oral liquids and creams; bind to polysorbates.
Alcohols and phenols: ethanol, benzyl alcohol, chlorobutanol, phenoxyethanol, phenol, chlorocresol (injections, multidose vials).

Quaternary ammonium compounds and others: benzalkonium chloride (eye drops, often with EDTA), cetrimide; chlorhexidine; organomercurials (thiomersal, phenylmercuric nitrate) in vaccines and eye drops.

Factors affecting preservative efficacy: pH and pKa, oil-water partition coefficient, binding to surfactants, polymers and suspended solids, sorption to containers and rubber, chemical incompatibility, temperature, type and number of contaminants; combinations give synergy and broader spectrum.

Preservative efficacy test (IP/BP/USP): separate containers of product inoculated with about 10^5-10^6 CFU/mL (or g) of Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli (oral), Candida albicans and Aspergillus brasiliensis; stored at 20-25°C protected from light.
Sampling: viable counts done at set times (e.g. 0, 6 h, 24 h, 7, 14 and 28 days, depending on pharmacopoeia and category) after neutralising preservative.

Acceptance: required log reduction of bacteria and fungi at each time for each product category (parenteral/ophthalmic stricter than oral or topical), e.g. for parenterals bacteria at least 2 log at 6 h, 3 log at 24 h and no recovery at 28 days (Ph. Eur. criterion A); no increase in fungi.
Microbial stability is also checked during stability studies by microbial limit tests and preservative content assay over shelf life.
a.diagram: Draw a graph of log CFU/mL (Y) vs time in days (X: 0, 7, 14, 28) with a falling line for a well-preserved product and a flat or rising line for a failed product; mark the required log reduction.
a.conclusion: Correct choice of preservative, attention to formulation interactions and a passing challenge test ensure microbial stability throughout the product's shelf life and in use.

mcq.q: Ribosomes found in the cytoplasm of bacteria are of which type?
mcq.explain: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S); eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S.

mcq.q: Teichoic acid is a characteristic component of the cell wall of:
mcq.explain: Teichoic and lipoteichoic acids are found in the thick peptidoglycan wall of Gram-positive bacteria.

mcq.q: In which phase of the growth curve is the generation time shortest and constant?
mcq.explain: Cells divide at a constant maximum rate in the log (exponential) phase.

mcq.q: Secondary metabolites such as antibiotics are mainly produced in the:
mcq.explain: Antibiotics and spores are typically produced when nutrients become limiting, in the stationary phase.

mcq.q: The catalyst used in the McIntosh and Fildes anaerobic jar is:
mcq.explain: Palladised alumina (palladium) catalyses combination of H2 with residual O2 to form water.

mcq.q: Which microscope is the method of choice for demonstrating Treponema pallidum in a fresh specimen?
mcq.explain: Treponema is too thin for bright field; dark field shows it as bright spirals on a dark background.

mcq.q: The most suitable method for long-term preservation of bacterial cultures is:
mcq.explain: Freeze drying (lyophilization) keeps cultures viable for many years in sealed ampoules.

mcq.q: Which method gives the viable count of bacteria?
mcq.explain: Only plate counts (CFU) measure living cells; the others count live and dead cells.

mcq.q: Agar used in culture media is obtained from:
mcq.explain: Agar is a polysaccharide extracted from red algae such as Gelidium; few bacteria degrade it.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a selective medium?
mcq.explain: Bile salts in MacConkey agar inhibit Gram-positive bacteria, making it selective (and differential).

mcq.q: In Gram staining, the step that differentiates Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria is:
mcq.explain: Decolouriser removes the crystal violet-iodine complex only from Gram-negative cells.

mcq.q: The IMViC pattern of Escherichia coli is:
mcq.explain: E. coli is indole +, methyl red +, Voges-Proskauer -, citrate -.

mcq.q: The biological indicator used to monitor moist heat sterilization is spores of:
mcq.explain: G. stearothermophilus spores are highly resistant to moist heat.

mcq.q: The biological indicator used for radiation sterilization is:
mcq.explain: Bacillus pumilus spores are used to monitor ionizing radiation cycles.

mcq.q: The Z-value is defined as the:
options: Temperature change needed to change the D-value by a factor of 10
mcq.explain: Z-value is the rise in temperature (°C) that reduces the D-value tenfold.

mcq.q: The Bowie-Dick test is used to check:
options: Air removal and steam penetration in an autoclave
mcq.explain: Bowie-Dick test pack shows uniform colour change only if air is removed properly.

mcq.q: The usual sterilizing dose of gamma radiation for medical products is:
mcq.explain: 25 kGy is the traditional standard dose for radiation sterilization.

mcq.q: Ethylene oxide kills microorganisms mainly by:
options: Alkylation of proteins and nucleic acids
mcq.explain: EtO is an alkylating agent acting on -SH, -NH2, -OH and -COOH groups.

mcq.q: In the Ziehl-Neelsen stain, acid-fast bacilli appear:
mcq.explain: Acid-fast cells retain carbol fuchsin (red); others take the methylene blue counterstain.

mcq.q: A sterility assurance level of 10^-6 means:
options: Six log reduction of bioburden only
Not more than one non-sterile unit in a million
mcq.explain: SAL is the probability of a viable organism surviving on one unit after sterilization.

mcq.q: The cell wall of fungi is mainly composed of:
mcq.explain: Fungal walls contain chitin and glucans; peptidoglycan is bacterial.

mcq.q: Candida albicans is best described as a:
mcq.explain: Candida reproduces by budding and forms pseudohyphae, so it is called yeast-like.

mcq.q: Influenza virus for vaccine production is traditionally grown in the:
mcq.explain: Influenza virus is grown in the allantoic cavity of embryonated hen's eggs.

mcq.q: Pocks on the chorioallantoic membrane are produced by:
mcq.explain: Poxviruses (variola, vaccinia) form visible pocks on the CAM.

mcq.q: The test organism used in the Rideal-Walker phenol coefficient test is:
mcq.explain: RW test uses Salmonella typhi; Chick-Martin uses S. typhi and S. aureus with organic matter.

mcq.q: A disinfectant with a high concentration exponent (e.g. phenol, n = 6) means:
options: It is unaffected by organic matter
Dilution has little effect on activity
mcq.explain: Activity falls by 2^n when concentration is halved; for n = 6 that is 64-fold.

mcq.q: In the IP sterility test, soybean-casein digest medium is incubated at:
mcq.explain: SCDM (fungi and aerobes) is incubated at 20-25°C; FTM at 30-35°C.

mcq.q: The membrane pore size used in the membrane filtration method of sterility testing is:
mcq.explain: Pharmacopoeias specify a membrane of nominal pore size not greater than 0.45 µm for the sterility test.

mcq.q: Which disinfectant is a high-level disinfectant capable of killing spores with sufficient contact time?
mcq.explain: Glutaraldehyde alkylates proteins and is sporicidal with prolonged exposure; QACs, alcohol and chlorhexidine are not.

mcq.q: Quaternary ammonium compounds are inactivated by:
mcq.explain: Cationic QACs are neutralised by anionic soaps, hard water and organic matter.

mcq.q: A HEPA filter removes at least what percentage of 0.3 µm particles?
mcq.explain: HEPA filters are rated at 99.97% efficiency for 0.3 µm particles.

mcq.q: Grade A clean area corresponds approximately to:
mcq.explain: Grade A (and Grade B at rest) correspond to ISO 5, the old Class 100.

mcq.q: The recommended air velocity of unidirectional airflow in a Grade A zone (EU GMP guidance) is about:
mcq.explain: EU GMP Annex 1 guidance value is 0.36-0.54 m/s at the working position.

mcq.q: The largest single source of contamination in an aseptic area is:
mcq.explain: Operators continuously shed skin particles carrying microbes.

mcq.q: Which laminar flow equipment protects the operator as well as the product?
mcq.explain: Class II BSCs have inflow and HEPA-filtered downflow and exhaust, protecting operator and product.

mcq.q: Vitamin B12 is assayed microbiologically using:
mcq.explain: L. leichmannii requires B12 for growth; its growth is proportional to B12 content.

mcq.q: In the cylinder-plate antibiotic assay, zone diameter is linearly related to the:
mcq.explain: Zone diameter vs log dose is a straight line in the working range.

mcq.q: The main advantage of the turbidimetric assay over the cylinder-plate method is:
mcq.explain: Turbidimetric assays need only about 3-4 h incubation versus 16-18 h for plates.

mcq.q: The pressure difference usually maintained between adjacent clean rooms of different grades is about:
mcq.explain: A cascade of about 10-15 Pa keeps air flowing from cleaner to less clean areas.

mcq.q: Media fill (process simulation) is used to validate:
mcq.explain: A growth medium is processed like the product to show aseptic filling does not contaminate units.

mcq.q: Benzoic acid is an effective preservative only at acidic pH because:

mcq.explain: Weak acid preservatives act in the unionised form, which predominates below their pKa (about 4.2).

mcq.q: Parabens lose preservative activity in the presence of:
mcq.explain: Parabens bind to non-ionic surfactant micelles, lowering the free concentration.

mcq.q: Which organism is NOT among the standard challenge organisms in the preservative efficacy test?
mcq.explain: Challenge organisms are S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, E. coli (oral), C. albicans and A. brasiliensis; C. sporogenes is used in sterility test controls.

mcq.q: Which dosage form is least susceptible to microbial spoilage?
mcq.explain: Very low water activity in anhydrous bases prevents microbial growth.

mcq.q: The normal diploid cell strains used for human vaccines, such as WI-38, can divide about:
mcq.explain: Finite diploid cells show the Hayflick limit of about 50 population doublings.

mcq.q: Which is a continuous (established) cell line widely used for recombinant protein production?
mcq.explain: Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells are immortal and used for monoclonal antibodies and other biologics.

mcq.q: Loss of contact inhibition and anchorage-independent growth are features of:
mcq.explain: Transformed cells grow over each other and in soft agar.

mcq.q: Animal cell cultures are commonly incubated in an atmosphere containing:
mcq.explain: 5% CO2 maintains the bicarbonate-buffered pH of the medium at about 7.2-7.4.

mcq.q: Which organism is a common cause of contamination in pharmaceutical water and eye drops?
mcq.explain: P. aeruginosa grows in water with minimal nutrients and causes serious eye infections.

mcq.q: The cryoprotectant commonly used for freezing animal cells is:
mcq.explain: 5-10% dimethyl sulfoxide (or glycerol) prevents ice crystal damage during freezing.
